strings.COL_Fall_Old_Republic: The Fall of the Old Republic
strings.COL_Fall_Old_Republic_desc:
The old order, flawed as it was, at least accomplished something none prior could: It forged a Republic, a nation-state that, despite its imperfections, guaranteed a semblance of peace and offered mechanisms for the peaceful evolution of law.

That order in tatters and in its stead chaos reigns. Corruption, banditry, cynicism, and addiction, the decay is omnipresent at every level. Even if the government were to escape its decade-long deadlock, it may be too late to undo the damage.
strings.COL_Paradise_City_desc:
Bogotá stands akin a a shining oasis. A city of steel and glass isolated from its burning landscape. It is the epicenter of political might, a densely populated sprawl of opulence, housing Colombia's industries and elite. On paper, it's a paradise. In reality, it rots under its overlord's watch.

Crime festers in the shadows and the streets are ruled through fear. Injustice weaves itself into the fabric of a society traumatized, and the promised potential of this grand metropolis slips further away, swallowed by the bleak reality of a country at war with itself.
strings.COL_Opium_Clouds_desc:
The introduction of Opium through the illegal smuggling markets of the Pacific and the discovery of recreational uses for marihuana in the northern coast have resulted in a widespread problem of growing demand for drugs and the consequences it has had for public health.

From miscarriages to overdose deaths, this demoralizing vice has transformed the life of the lower classes in the republic to a limitless search for satisfaction, and their environments in cruel mixes of violence and exploitation.

Yet addiction is merely a symptom, a way for the meager man to distract himself from the unforgiving reality that waits outside their door.
strings.COL_Fields_Opportunity_desc:
The decrepit state of the Republic can best be observed in its benign ignorance of the state of affairs in its rural territories. With the government's influence contracting, paramilitaries and bandits have taken to ruling the countryside in the name of their betters, or merely their greed.

With the façade removed, violent acquisitions have become merely a sliver of the ruthless displayed by the new unstable yet rather profitable state of affairs. For though they may have been banished from the halls of power, the landed classes of old have not conceded their claim to them.

In due time they will return, the only question is whose banner will they pretend carry when that day comes.
strings.COL_Fallen_Colossus_desc:
As Colombia's most storied, professional, and enduring institution, it was only natural that its state of affairs would evolve as well. The once celebrated honor and gallantry of the armed forces fades away, eclipsed by an increasing reliance on crude violence and political campaigns to maintain its privileged place in society.

Yet in many ways, the Colossus could not adapt. Despite its enduring superiority to untrained militias, the army now stands as a cumbersome relic. One expensive to sustain, sluggish to mobilize, and plagued with evils deep within its once cherished soul.
strings.COL_Guardians_Peace_desc:
Reform of the Armed Forces had long been thought of as a necessity, yet none had hoped for it to have occurred this way. The failed coup by General Pinilla and his cronies forced a purge of Armed Forces.

With its numbers pared down, the Colossus was easily conquered and transformed into a a more professional and apolitical force. Efforts to expand the scope of the reform to include modernization bore an unexpected success thanks to a renewal of American support.

Now it is time for a live fire test.
strings.COL_Grand_Army_Republic: The Grand Army of the Republic
strings.COL_Grand_Army_Republic_desc:
Since the birth of the first Republic, the scornful elites of Colombia have schemed to secure power for themselves, casting shadows over Bolívar's grand project. Their power grabs and hungry maneuvering have only deepened the wounds inflicted by the ruptures of 1831 and 1903. Now they threaten to destroy the remaining shreds of the vision of unity, integrity, and justice that Colombia was designed to be.

Under General Pinilla's watchful gaze, this fallen colossus has been more than rejuvenated. With unmatched manpower and a will forged in the fires of conviction, the Grand Army is ready to march once more, prepared to end the schemes of those who would see The Republic fall. Like a storm of fire, like nature's wrath unleashed, it will cleanse the fields, leaving no trace of its enemies. The republic shall stand anew, guarded not merely on the battlefield, but in the halls of power as well.
strings.COL_Holy_Knights_desc:
Colombia's gravest mistake has been its departure from the side of Christ, a betrayal set in motion by liberalism and secularism since the Rionegro Constitution of 1863. This forsaking of divine allegiance shattered the vision of a grand nation—a bastion strong enough to guard freedom in the New World—and reduced it to a weakened sovereignty, vulnerable to even the slightest organized threat.

In answer, the rejuvenated Conservative Hegemony has reshaped it in Christ's image, as a faithful legion dedicated to an unending crusade for peace and order in the realm of the Sacred Heart. Each soldier now stands as a knight of a holy cause, commissioned to serve not merely with weapons, but with the armor of a devout heart and the fire of unwavering faith.
strings.COL_The_Collapse_of_Colombo_American_Cor: Colombia and the United States have never been this distant, ever since the neutrality declaration of 1940 and our negative to participate in the American war effort, tensions began to rise between the two nations, culminating in the definite collapse of diplomatic relations by 1956 when the last American diplomat was recalled from Bogotá, leaving the question of diplomatic proximity with our old partner open for the national government to discuss.
strings.COL_Off_to_a_Fresh_Start_desc: After a successful negotiations process, the United States and Colombia have restored their relations in full and a bright future awaits for this newfound friendship.
strings.COL_Colombo_American_Treaty_on_Friendshi: Colombo-American Treaty on Friendship and Diplomatic Cordiality

Our coordinated efforts resulted in the restoration of relations with the US in an almost complete level, with most of the pressing issues of our agendas being successfully conciliated, a healthy relationship begins to be consolidated.
strings.COL_Leaving_past_Grudges_Behind_desc: After the negotiations, an initial settlement with the United States of America has been worked out, and while there is still a long agenda ahead of us, it's with great hope that we can say that the rebuilding of our friendship has begun.
strings.COL_Large_Scale_Offensive_desc: With the restart of hostilities in Colombia, the factions involved in the civil war have intensified the offensive with the support of their foreign patrons. The conflict rages across the mountains and the jungles, until only one faction remains.
strings.COL_Shoulders_of_Giants_desc:
To understand the reasons why Colombia burns, one must look to three souls whose legacy is the violence that now unfolds.

While elsewhere in the nation, the assassination of Gaitán is mourned, in New Granada a requiem for a different man. Mariano Ospina Pérez, grand eminence of Conservatism, proud stalwart against the false promises of Laureanism. A man slain, hanged in the Capital's square by a mob whom the Duce and his compatriots yet claim to have its thirst for blood unsatiated.

An amusing coincidence then, for all their differences, a common chant unites Conservatives, Liberals and Socialists: Death to the lackeys of the false prophet Laureano Goméz. Death to their far-off backers in Germania and Madrid. Death to the old order.

Veritias Vincit.
strings.COL_Saints_Sinners: A War of Saints and Sinners
strings.COL_Saints_Sinners_desc:
The radicalization brought on by La Violencia has carved a great divide within Colombian society. While many wars can claim to be brother against brother, few come close to the radicalization and dehumanization that has been plaguing Colombian society since the mid 50s. The sheer vehement for those they fight and the ignorance towards their own champion's crimes has reached a level where the war itself can be likened to one of Saints and Sinners.

Pillaging, banditry and murder are a common and ignored sight on every front. Yet regardless of the contender observed, a common element within the narrative remains, the war that ravages this country will be one fought to the death.
strings.COL_Eastern_Frontier_desc:
The victory over the Revolutionary Front has proven to be a pyrrhic one indeed. In ousting them from Tunja, we have only managed to push them further into entrenched jungle positions. In tearing apart their frontline, we have ensured pockets of resistance all across the East. And In executing their leaders, we have only further enraged what soldiers survived.

The testament to this “victory” is the newly inaugurated Comisaría del Oriente. A Military Government put in charge to pacify thousands of kilometers and given the means to throw as many men into the Sovereign East as needed. Make no mistake, the Colombian Civil War has not ended, it has only transitioned to a new phase.

strings.COL_USA_negotiation.0.desc:
It was rarely ever not a busy day at the US State Department, but some days would throw curveballs at you in more interesting ways than usual. Today, the Secretary of State found himself reading a proposal from the Brazilians on the Colombian Crisis: to ditch the Revolutionaries sweating it out in the jungle in favor of the new Bogotá government. Officially, relations between the United States and the Colombian government had frozen for years, and contact between the two had been formally severed since 1957. Brazil's offer to act as an intermediary was surprising but welcome to those with reservations about arming socialist Revolutionaries.

As such, the Secretary had drawn up a list of proposals for the new Colombian government, to show that they could play ball and distance themselves from the fascist dictatorship they replaced. He took a moment to read over a short version of the list, namely the two most important pieces: the first, a public denouncement of Germania. That, hopefully, was going to be the easy part. The second was compensation for nationalized American assets. That would be the much more difficult of the two.

The Colombians, doubtlessly, would have requests of their own, but the Secretary was satisfied with what he had, for now. He then jotted down another note to himself: put Lincoln Gordon and his staff in charge of the negotiations, and get him a line to their FBI agent inside the Brazilian embassy in Bogotá.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.0.a: Gordon's a smart man; he can get it done.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.1.desc:
Officially, the USA had withdrawn all personnel from the Colombian mainland since it recalled its ambassador in 1957. Unofficially, it has maintained several contacts and agents across the country, most importantly, the FBI. For Gordon Lincoln, his contact would be a man stationed inside the Brazilian embassy. “Hola, sí, sí, soy Lincoln. Necesito hablar con William. Sí, esperaré en línea.”

Barely a minute had passed before a distinctly American accent came onto the line. “William speaking. I understand you have some requests?”

“So to speak.” Gordon hummed. “The United States is interested in renewing its relationship with Colombia, with some requirements.”

“Of course. To ensure a smooth discussion, I recommend bringing forth these issues one at a time.”

“My thoughts exactly. As such, I figured we'd start with something simple: a public denouncement of Germany and its so-called Unity Pact.”

“Hmm. I can see the government accepting this. Few men hold the Laureanists and their Germanophilia in high regard. Though I'm certain you understand, we most certainly cannot afford to cast out what aid comes our way without finding a new source first.”
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.1.a: “Let's hope he makes the right choice.”
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.1.ttt: The Governing Coalition's furthest right elements will be weakened if @COL Colombia accepts.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.3.desc:
Brasília's warm breath fogged up the windows of the embassy and sprayed crystal dewdrops in the leaves. Lincoln Gordon took to the front steps, coffee cup in hand, and found the American and Brazilian staff passing around the morning newspaper. He waited his turn to fumble with the pages.

“How are the Portuguese lessons going? Won't be able to enjoy O Globo much if you can't read,” a colleague said with a bump of the shoulder.

“We're getting there.” Gordon shook his head, scanning the stories, and there he found it.

“LÍDER COLOMBIANO DENUNCIA GERMANIA.”

There was a picture of the Colombian delegation attached, and while his colleague offered to translate, Gordon politely waved him off for later. A more detailed report would be necessary, of course, but he understood that headline well enough. Bogotá had done the expected and followed American advice, and all was well with the world for now. He smiled, really breathed in that roasted aroma of his coffee, and passed the newspaper to the next guy.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.3.a: Expected or not, a man can be happy for successes.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.4.desc:
A cable from the Colombian embassy, Mr. President.“

Normally, {bra_getleader} would have waved away any aides when eating his lunch, but this had been a long-expected one. He set down his forkful of rice and motioned for the message to read.

”The Colombian government has officially denounced Germania for its involvement in Colombian affairs, including its meddling in the civic conflict.“ {bra_getleader} read aloud with a broadening smile, shoulders looser. He read over the reaction from the Americans, who were quite pleased of course, and imagined the Germans' fuming.

Bogotá had, as hoped, turned out to be the right fit for Brazil's, and by extension, American, interests. He was the right horse to back indeed. {bra_getleader} thanked his aide, already thinking of the next stages in the diplomatic offensive in Bogotá. At least, he was glad his lunch wasn't ruined.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.4.a: Everything tastes sweeter with a side of victory.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.5.desc:
The news of developments in Colombia reached Alvorada Palace faster than the rest of Brasília, or, for that matter, the rest of the world. That was how {bra_getleader} learned the magnitude of the mess before anyone else.

“The Colombians are categorically refusing to issue any statements that rile up the Germans,” the cables from Bogotá said. “U.S. negotiators are frustrated. We are at an impasse.”

{bra_getleader} wondered where this subservient Colombia, which wouldn't dare offend the Germans helping destroy his country, went when it was time to negotiate with Brazil. He wondered, too, if Brazil had picked the wrong horse when it chose to back him over the Gaitanists.

“If it were the Gaitanists, we wouldn't even be discussing Germany,” {bra_getleader} muttered.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.5.a: We make do with past choices, wrong or not.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.6.desc:
A late-at-night phone ring was never a good omen. In the back of his neck, Lincoln Gordon expected sudden bad news as he picked up, and William's sigh on the other end of the line confirmed it.

“You can't be serious.”

“Believe me, I wish I wasn't,” William said. “They've refused. Bogotá's stalled and rejected our offers so far. Won't break with the Germans.”

“The same Germans shoring up the opponents that want to kill them,” Gordon muttered.

“Running theory's they're more dependent on the Führer's purse than we thought.” And it was so absurd that Gordon would have laughed if he wasn't going to get strung up by the balls in Washington over it.

The ambassador seemed to notice the bags under his eyes the next morning, and he contacted the Brazilians first thing.

“It was their idea to negotiate with Bogotá, so they better have a Plan B for this,” Gordon warned, and the ambassador fidgeted with his collar.

“They say we continue the negotiations. Stay the course until Bogotá accedes, and it will accede.”

“Stay the course...” He held back a bitter comment. It wasn't Brasília who would look bad to his superiors if Colombia couldn't be cowed. Still, what did he get from complaining?
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.6.a: One way or another, Colombia would stop eating from the hand that beat it.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.7.desc:
William read over the instructions from the State Department with a thin expression. Seems they were insisting on compensation for nationalized assets, namely, branch offices seized by the Laureanists back in the 50s, an event that was a major reason American-Colombian relations fell apart.

The State Department's demand would be a very difficult one, one that would bring up a lot of bad memories for both sides, especially with a man like {col_getleader} in charge. From everything that he had gathered about Colombia's new leader, the nationalization of foreign assets was one of the few things he and the Laureanists seemed to agree on, and he wasn't going to bend on the matter easily.

Still, the matter was important if their governments were to reach an agreement. Hopefully, Bogotá's sense of self-preservation would outweigh its ideological dedications.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.8.desc:
When one is the Chancellor of the Imaraty Palace, one tends to learn a few things. One of the less comfortable realizations is how little sleep one gets on the job. One of the more distressing of these realizations is that diplomacy among great powers is a dying art, and the sheer volume of tacklessness they can condense into a single message is almost impressive.

The Yankees demanded that every company nationalized by the Colombian government return to American hands as quickly as possible. It was as ridiculous as it was insulting, and {col_getleader}, whatever his faults, wouldn't be in the wrong if he stood his ground against something so humiliating. The Chancellor drummed one hand on their desk, considering alternatives.

Bogotá would balk at compensation for all assets, but negotiations didn't have to end there. Perhaps if {col_getleader} stood his ground against total compensation, but with a counteroffer in mind, a compromise could be made. Of course, the Americans wouldn't be pleased by such a thing. Gingerly, the Chancellor reaches for the phone.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.8.a: Advise Bogotá to make a counteroffer.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.10.desc:
“Just got word back from Bogotá, he says that we're asking for too much-” William began, his voice broken up by some mild crackling, “but he's willing to meet us halfway.”

Gordon heaved a sigh. “Define what you mean by 'halfway,' please.” If Bogotá's latest protagonist wasn't going to give him a headache, he had a feeling that the State Department's response would.

“Ah, well, he's willing to give back some of the shares of all the companies that were nationalized.” William paused to let the words sink in before continuing. “He insists that they will be vital for post-war reconstruction, and that Colombia cannot afford to return it all.”

Admittedly, the deal would still be better than getting nothing. Didn't change the fact that the Palacio de Nariño's continued defiance was going to ruffle a lot of feathers. Gordon mulled over the potential consequences before making his choice.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.10.a: “Alright, let him know we can meet halfway too.”
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.10.b: “Tell him it's happening our way, or not at all.”
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.11.desc:
William grimaced as he wrote up his latest report on the negotiations with the Central Government. The Brazilians had sent him the State Department's demands for compensation, or at least a watered-down version. Didn't matter much either way, because the Casa de Nariño had refused, rather decisively too: the Colombian government would not, under any circumstances, return American assets they seized control of.

William could already imagine the reaction from Gordon and the rest of the State Department: indignation, outrage. Wouldn't surprise him if some of them wanted to end negotiations right here. Whatever the case, this was going to be a serious setback, and Bogotá was going to need to act carefully if they still wanted American aid.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.11.a: Better get those phone calls over with...
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.12.desc:
He actually had done it.

Lincoln Gordon was just as blown away from actually reading the affidavit in his hands as when William told him ahead of time over the phone, the call ending right as the piece of paper wound up in his lap at his office in the Embassy in Brasília. By every measure, this was meant to be a unilaterally good thing, at least for Washington, and yet...

{col_getleader} could beat his chest all he liked and have every state-run propaganda outlet paint him as the second coming of Bolívar, but most people already knew the score. No political or military leader had a regime beyond reproach. Not the Colombians, not the Spanish or the Portuguese, not the Italians or even the Germans. There was always someone reliably picking away, little by little, at the underpinnings of the government.

All the more reason, Gordon presumed, that Bogotá had finally knuckled under the American demands. American former assets in Colombia, the very same ones {col_getleader} had ordered nationalized, were to be summarily returned without complaint. At least, without complaint from {col_getleader} himself, or at least none he was willing to say publicly.

There was perhaps a chance that Gordon was overthinking it. It could have been a genuine attempt to parlay in the negotiations as an act of good faith, if for no other reason than to give himself leverage. Nonetheless, the US regaining control over their assets in Colombia was a great windfall. Assuming, at the very least, the negotiations continued in Washington's favor.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.12.a: An attempt at detente or the beginnings of a plea bargain?
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.14.desc:
The President's office at the Planalto greeted the news with quiet relief, a rare thing in the world of South American geopolitics. Both {bra_getleader} and the Itamaratay Councilor were going to have their hands full, but assuming everything went smoothly, Brasília and her allies in Washington might be able to actually get something out of Bogotá for once.

The Government's demands were relatively straightforward: Colombian sovereignty over San Andrés and its surrounding archipelago. A reasonable demand, considering they used to be a Colombian territory until the Yankees seized it at the start of La Violencia. A less reasonable demand considering the archipelago's natives wanted nothing to do with Bogotá anymore. Still, if this was the carrot to ply the Republic's supporters in Bogotá, the parties involved could work with that.

At the behest of {bra_getleader}, phone calls were made to the Itamaratay in Rio to begin the processes of the Caribbean handover. One might say Brasília could use a win like this and not just for cooler relations with Colombia. Common perception of Brazil's role in the OFN is hard to disentangle from the image of Brazil being a sock-puppet for American interests in the region. Hopefully, with their role in ironing out the agreement with {col_getleader}, Brazil's leaders could live down some of this stigma and further legitimize themselves as a proper partner in affirming OFN affairs in South America.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.14.a: Hopefully, we can get this done.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.14.tt: San Andrés and Providencia will be returned to @COLColombia after the end of the Colombian Civil War.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.15.desc:
“Mr. Secretary, Bogotá is seeking the return of San Andrés and Providencia.”

“I'll need a bit more context. What are the Brazilians saying? Where even are San Andrés and Providencia? What's the Colombian claim? Why are we there?”

“My apologies, Mr. Secretary, we haven't had time to draft a formal report. San Andrés and Providencia are a Caribbean archipelago - located closer to Nicaragua than Colombia, but Nicaragua recognized the latter's claim in a 1928 treaty. As La Violencia worsened, we occupied the islands to preserve order and prevent criminality after Bogotá lost any ability to project authority that far afield. The islands are lightly populated and have limited strategic or economic value - primarily just a tourist destination. Itamaratay is pushing hard for the handover, saying that returning the land will improve our reputation across the Americas.”

“Make Brazil look good in the process, I suppose. Well - get me that report and let me know if any Senators will take issue with giving back the archipelago. On the condition that they put a definitive end to their civil war and... and they keep on good behavior.”

“Yes, Mr. Secretary, several Senators have in fact-”
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.15.a: “Unless that report says otherwise, start prepping for their eventual return.”
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.15.b: “Then we hold on to the San Andes or whatever they're called. Send me the report as a formality.”
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.16.t: Uncle Sam Rolls the Iron Dice
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.16.desc:
The image of the Casa de Nariño slowly disappeared in the rearview mirror as the state car rolled along the streets of Bogotá, with nothing but {col_getleader}'s own words echoing in William's head. As far as the deal was concerned, everything seemed to be in place. Brazil had given official recognition, the US had (mostly) given the green light, and now {col_getleader} had seemingly finalized it.

Even the Colombian military was enthusiastic about the agreement, something that was rare in William's own dealings with Bogotá. He even received a formal invitation to dinner, a great honor, but William had other obligations. Clearly, Bogotá was at least somewhat genuine in its commitment to the American alliance; better still, Colombia would be gaining territory in the Caribbean in the process.

This was all still preliminary however, even as the metaphorical ink on the agreement was still wet. The Civil War was still raging, and even if Bogotá came out on top, leftist partisans and Axis-backed belligerents would likely still be a problem for years after. The beleaguered central government would likely lean on the US for aid in that effort too, but for now, {col_getleader}'s regime was on the march.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.16.a: Washington's heirs have thrown in with Bolívar's disciple.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.17.desc:
OFN MANDATE TO MAINTAIN CONTROL OF DISPUTED ISLANDS

As soon as William looked over the article, he could hear the upcoming speech blaring over the radio. The United States had interpreted Pinilla's request for the islands to be returned as a step too far. The response had been relatively delicate in its wording, and had even officially recognised his continued primacy over the island, but the statement, warning of continued instability and of regional security needs, might as well have been written in blood.

“Once again, the Americans have shown their contempt for Colombia's integrity,” roared Pinilla, his rage burning through the speaker. “My efforts to simply return the islands unjustly occupied by the United States have failed, and they shall remain as such for far longer. Washington claims that they will safeguard it from the tyranny of national socialism, but their teeth glint with the light of their dagger as they hunger for the right to partition yet more parts of Colombia.”

He sighed, turning down the radio. Of course, the Brazilians would also be frustrated. He wasn't fluent in Portuguese, but he didn't need that to know just how many promises Brasilia had been delivering to him in return for his offer. Whether they included the direct promise or not, he knew what side they'd be taking, and that he'd be expected in Rio within the week. There was nothing he could do, he thought, except prepare himself for the upcoming outrage that both sides would present him with.

“Many people have abandoned you, but I have not. These islands may still be occupied for now, yet as much as I know that Colombia is not fated to eternal civil war, I know that San Andrés and Providencia are not fated to occupation. I will continue to work diligently to ensure they are returned, and will continue to fight for the unification of Colombia by any means necessary.”
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.17.a: A promise of violence delivered for the fight ahead.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.18.t: A Letter of Disdain for Washington
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.18.desc:
FROM: ITAMARY PALACE OF THE UNITED STATES OF BRAZIL

TO: SECRETARY OF STATE OF THE UNITED STATES

TOPIC: RETURN OF THE SAN ANDRÉS AND PROVEDENCIA ISLANDS

We are deeply concerned at the continued Mandate over Colombian territories. Since independence, these have legally been part of the Colombian government, and have repeatedly presented their underlying loyalties to the state of Colombia despite past efforts to transfer these territories to Panama.

Colombia may be facing unrest, but that alone is not cause to seize territory. The legal President of Colombia still governs a significant portion of the country, including the capital of Bogotá. There is no legal framework, beyond that of the Rome-Berlin Axis, that justifies this occupation, beyond some vague overtures for stability.

The Bogotá government has been willing to engage with the United States of America and with Brazil, and has opened up negotiations with the Organisation of Free Nations. Its demands are not excessive, and have come solely out of a desire to unify their own country. The US occupation of these islands will weaken their claim, and will hamper their efforts at restoring stability.

Although the American government might not recognize the claim, Brazil remains a staunch ally of Colombia, and will continue to treat this occupation as both illegal and arbitrary. We stand behind the Colombian government in its efforts at restoring control over the country, and warn the United States that further violations of sovereignty in Latin America will come with consequences.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.18.a: A united front comes from far below.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.19.desc:
“Thank you for your time,” said {col_getleader}, “but I have one last request. I believe you already know what it is.” The Secretary of State nodded, as he adjusted the quimbaya that {col_getleader} gave him as a gift. It was one of many knick knacks that adorned the office.

{col_getleader} continued, “As we're the central government of Colombia, and our civil war is over, I believe it is only right for us to be readmitted to the Organization of American States”

The two sat in silence for a moment, the Secretary of State tapped his pen on the table. {col_getleader} knew that his demand was a big one, but it made sense. All the radicals were gone and {col_getleader} was certainly not the worst candidate to win. Those New Grenadine freaks wouldn't have made it to the US let alone Foggy Bottom.

The Secretary of State spoke, “I believe we can accept your reentry.” {col_getleader} smiled and thanked the Secretary of State. “Thank you, sir.” With that {col_getleader} smiled and left, excited to return to Bogotá.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.19.a: And with that, Colombia returns to the fold.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.19.a.tt: @COL Colombia shall join the Organization of American States!
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.19.b: But it was all a lie.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.20.desc:
For a few weeks, {bra_getleader} had thought the northern border had been surprisingly quiet. Since the dispute over the San Andrés and Providencia Islands had been settled, the Itamaraty Chancellery had mostly moved onto other pressing matters as Bogotá fell silent once more. As the knock came, followed by a familiar tone, {bra_getleader} knew this short reprieve was over.

“Bogotá wants to rejoin the Organization of American States,” responded the Chancellor, thumbing through a folder to bring out the most relevant document. “Of course, nothing within the message should be surprising. An internationally recognized government friendly to the United States and to diplomacy wants the prestige and to take part in the broader forum.”

{bra_getleader} raised an eyebrow, his eyes glazing over the file. “I don't see the problem with this. It's not like we'll be admitting the Gaitanists or fascists; we could easily suspend Colombia again if they come to power. Have the Americans responded to this request at all?”

“Bogotá and Washington both reached out to us yesterday,” he responded, hesitantly, “and Washington seemed to be noncommittal while Colombia's still unstable, but they didn't reject the idea outright. They know our stance, and they wouldn't mention it to us if they fully wanted to reject it.”

{bra_getleader} shook his head. “I can understand their fears, but if we stay silent for too long, then Bogotá's team will take this public and jeopardize any negotiations.”

“If it's uncertain, then we should privately assure the Colombians of our support. Obviously, making this public now would be a non-starter, but if we reach out to the Casa de Nariño privately, we should be able to buy ourselves enough time to swing the Americans onboard.”
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.20.a: Modesty, in this circumstance, is the best policy.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.21.desc:
The shrill ringing of the phone seemed to shake Lincoln Gordon from his stupor, his eyes open yet consciousness only returning as his limbic system sensed new stimulation. His tired eyes peered up. Had he been asleep? He looked at the report in his hands, the paper limply fallen back. 'Brazil-Africa Shipping Lane Incidents', dated to the previous three months. When was the last time he had even read a sentence? He shook his head. The barely-read report was thrust on the desk before him as he picked up the receiver. He needed to get some sleep.

“Gordan? William. I don't have much time, so I'll be brief. Bogotá is very satisfied with the prospect of OAS membership reinstatement, doubly so with its public US support. The word amongst our guys is that we are on the brink of our breakthrough.”

Lincoln smiled, placing the receiver on his other ear and balancing it with his shoulder as he reached for a notepad and pen. “Understood, thank you very much. Do you have any information on how quickly the Colombians are intending to move on this?”

“Aides in the Colombian camp told associates of mine that the mood amongst their representatives is positive, enthusiastic even. From what I have seen, they are eager to move forward as soon as we are. No one outside the circle of trust seems aware of these conversations yet.” Lincoln scrawled down the exact wording of his FBI man.

“Noted. I shall communicate this to Washington immediately. Stand by, Mr. William, it may be a late night.” Lincoln lowered the receiver with a smile, looking at the scrawled notation. His tired stupor seemed so distant now, in a second dissipated. He looked at the clock on his wall: just past two. In Washington, it was around midnight. The Secretary was probably asleep by now, or similarly beleaguered by the demands of fatigue.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.21.a: But who could turn down a nightcap such as this?
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.22.desc:
Lincoln Gordon might have been in the offices of the American embassy in Brasília, but for the past few hours, his phone had sounded no different than if he was in Bogotá. With the United States fully rejecting the possibility of admitting Colombia back into the Organisation of American States, Pinilla had become hostile, launching into tirades at any diplomat he saw. As the phone rang, Gordon felt some concern as he picked it up.

“Hello, this is Lincoln Gordon. Who is this?”

“This is President Rojas Pinilla”, spat the receiver, “President of the Republic of Colombia.”Gordon breathlessly sighed, holding it further from his ears. “I presume this is about the negotiations on the Or-”

“Yes, and I would very much like answers. We have been open to cooperation, and the compensation I've had in return is to be relegated to the stature of the rebels trying to collapse this country!”

“Look, I'm not the man to ask here. I had no involvement in the deal whatsoever, you'll have to reach out to the American consulate in Bogotá for an-”

“I know how powerful a man you are in Brazil. I know they were meant to come out on our behalf. I really doubt you can't push things further.”

Gordon struggled to give an answer. He knew how bad the situation in Colombia could get, and that it could happen too quickly for him to justify letting them back in. But he knew how delicate these talks were, and knew how much progress could have been lost. “That kind of news doesn't come down to my offices until a few hours after the President gives a speech. I'm afraid you'll have to talk to diplomats elsewhere.” A simple grunt was all that he received in return before the phone line shut off.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.24.desc:
It was early in the morning in the Palacio do Planalto, the warm, orange hue of the sunrise obscured by clouds in the distant horizon. Sipping from a mug of coffee, Henrique Lott took a minute to allow recent difficulties to linger elsewhere, at least momentarily.

“Do you remember the days of Floriano Peixito, Henrique?” asked Jair Dantas Riberio, taking out a cigar.

Lott simply chuckled at the question. “I'm not that much older than you, Jair, careful with those questions,” he sighed as he put down his glass, “but his legacy is still visible today. Without his careful hand guiding Brazil through those years, the Maragatos and naval officers would've torn this country apart. But why do you bring him up?”

“I was just thinking,” replied Riberio, turning his head to waft the smoke away, “Gustavo Rojas Pinilla. He's made a lot of progress since his coup. Bogotá's firmly under his grasp, he's internationally respected, and by the Americans, too. Give him a few years, and he could very well be the Colombian Iron Marshall.”

Lott thought for a moment, and then shook his head. “I wish that was the case, Ribeiro. I've spoken with the man a lot, and his ambitions go far further than that. He always talks with excitement at projects in ten, fifteen, twenty years. Might even live long enough to see them finish.” Clasping his fingers, Lott leant forwards. “He's too powerful to resign. Not if he can help it.”

Ribeiro looked surprised at the development. “That is a worry, but Floriano never faced this level of strife.” He took another draw for his cigar, his head remaining forwards. “Whatever happens, it's not up to us to decide his fate. The Colombians have reason standing alongside anarchy, and it's up to them to decide which direction they want to go in.”
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.24.a: The mirror glistens, but does it reflect Cincinattus or Caesar?
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.25.desc:
It was late at night, but the flickers of the lamp above failed to sweep away Lacerda's conscience. He looked over the documents in front of him once again, all the files on Colombia that hadn't been burnt after a single call. They repeated the same points again, discussing Rojas Pinilla's background, his coup, his government's composition, and yet he scoured them again, hoping for some new meaning. As he let one fall back onto the table, he accepted an unchanged defeat once again.

Colombia was, as ever, a mess. Pinilla's state had been gathering momentum, but how could he delude himself to view the violence as being over? The Gaitanists remained as dangerous as ever, striking a red dagger through the head of the Amazon. Gilberto Avedaño's forces continued to limp on, holding onto his fiefdoms in the far west and looking hungrily east. Pinilla's forces were the last ones standing for sanity against the radicalism of its opposition, an accolade that should have long earned his respect.

And yet, his heart lingered. He had read the reports of Pinilla's ambitions, and they didn't stop at the civil war. Executions of moderate dissidents in the coup, and of journalists being disappeared for “sedition” sat uneasy. Too close for comfort for him; scarcely a decade ago, he could've easily met the same fate. The moment that the last partisan forces were swept up, he knew that Pinilla would simply secure his place as one of an assortment of dictators plaguing the continent.

Lacerda sighed, looking outside to watch the Moon. He had made his decision long ago. If he wanted Pinilla to be powerless, the time to ensure that had long since passed. There was more to Pinilla's regime than the man himself, and there were still a few liberals, biding their time until peace to assert their authority. With American and Brazilian backing, perhaps that regime may, in another few decades, move from an unstable dictatorship to a fractured democracy.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.25.a: The Devil went down from Georgia, looking for a soul...
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.26.desc:
Bored, William flicked through a book, waiting in his apartment. It was a crime novel from the 1920s, a detective investigating murders between two Mafia families whilst vying for recognition from his boss amidst prohibition. Nothing more than a dime novel picked up from a random stall, really, but it was the first English he'd seen in weeks beyond State Department missives, and so its sheer novelty brought his gaze. Just as he turned the page, a ring came from behind him.

“Hello, William?” asked Gordon, pausing only to breathe. “I wanted to tell you that your job is done. Everything's gone through.”

William's eyes shot up. “The meeting went well, then?”

“As well as you could've hoped. It'll take a few more days and a press conference to be made official, but {usa_getleader} agreed that Bogotá is the best faction in Colombia, and is willing to recognize their government and send aid.”

William smiled, leaning in. “Great to hear, Gordon! I'm glad that our work has helped bring the President to the right side of the matter.” He pushed his chair back slightly, and then stopped. “Is there anything I need to do before returning to Washington?”

“Not yet, William. Bogotá's hold is still tenuous, and things could easily get out of hand. You're going to remain active in Colombia and in solidifying the central government's influence. I hope you understand.”

William tried to respond, but found himself immediately hung up on. Still, he took it in his stride. He was obviously successful and had been entrusted to work further with relative liberty. With nothing else to do, he turned back to his novel, reading as the detective gave chase, and then caught the patriarch of one family.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.26.a: That'll be a pay raise for sure!
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.27.desc:
The ringing of the phone on his desk snapped Lott out of the work he had been concentrating on. He realized it was late enough in the day that his office had grown quite dark despite the sun still being out, and so he turned on a lamp as he picked up the phone. Lott heard his secretary on the other end. “Mr. President, the ambassador to Colombia says he has urgent news he must speak to you about. Shall I direct him to your desk?”

“Send him through,” replied Lott. If all went well, this could be a great boon to the future security of both the OFN and Brazil. After he heard the ambassador greet him on the other end of the line, Lott asked, “What's the status of the negotiations with Bogotá?”

“The Colombians walked out, and Washington's thrown in the towel. The negotiations are over,” replied the ambassador. With a tired sigh, Lott dismissed the ambassador and hung up the phone.

Lott couldn't say that he was entirely shocked by this outcome; he expected that the negotiations might be rocky. Still didn't make it any less frustrating that they couldn't see the forest for the trees. Nor was Lott particularly enthusiastic regarding the alternative he was now forced to pursue.

With a heavy hand illuminated only by the desklamp's dim light, Lott began drafting up a new set of orders. With Republic removing themselves off the table, the only option left would be the Gaitanists, and now Brazil had no choice but to throw its support behind their cause.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.28.desc:
Lacerda stared blankly at the painting hanging behind his desk. It was a modernist piece of art, depicting a man holding a guitar. At the moment, the painting elicited no feelings within Lacerda. The technical work was well-executed, but the only impact the painting held over Lacerda was allowing him to not think about reality for a brief moment longer.

Lacerda let out an exasperated groan. The Colombians had walked away from the negotiations. There was no going back now, and the Americans would be supporting those Red Caudillos in Eastern Colombia. America and Brazil would be supporting the spread of socialism all because Bogotá had walked away.

There'd be no saviors for Colombia, the country would merely burn itself to the ground to determine which arsonists would get to rule the ashes, with Brazil and America footing the bill. The more he thought about it, the angrier Lacerda got. His temple was already throbbing, and as Lacerda realized he was going to have to explain all of this all over again to Golbery, the throbbing transformed into a full-blown headache.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.29.desc:
It was deep into night, the only light coming from the Moon and emanating from the light above. Under the cover of near-total silence wrought by worry, he searched the flat for anything he had left behind. He couldn't afford to leave anything behind, at least not for the next few days. Opening a cabinet, he found a briefing on intercepted troop movements hidden within. Whatever operative was gathering the information would be damned if it came out, especially now.

Where had it gone wrong? He folded a shirt into his briefcase. Obviously, the terms had not been negotiated well. The United States couldn't just concede everything, especially to a faction within a civil war. But surely one or two more concessions wouldn't have hurt? The Colombian government was not fundamentally anathema to the United States. They could have easily negotiated down, reduced the most radical point, and survived. Did the United States really need to hold onto the San Andrés islands?

They clearly needed to now. As he made one final check through the flat, his mind was clear. Washington would publish a statement condemning Colombian action tomorrow. How long the condemnation would be depended on whether any diplomats were arrested, but it was coming. Then, they would quietly start funnelling weaponry elsewhere. The fascists of New Granada were obviously unviable, both in morality and alignment, and so the only clear alternative left was the Gaitanists of Guadeloupe Salcedo.

Shutting the door behind him, he debated whether or not to leave his key before choosing to keep it. They probably wouldn't go so far to check a copy of it, he reasoned. Not that they'd be able to do much anyway, even if they were. Within the day, he'd be down to Bucarramanga, and then rural Santander. There, his mediator would make contact with a group of Gaitanists, where they'd discuss terms, offer promises and, hopefully, await pickup. Creeping outside, a van honked, and he turned to enter.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.30.desc:
It had been a long few days, and now, the diplomat struggled in bed. Overstretched by several busy days and now struck with the flu, he could do little else but lie there, reflecting on the course of the negotiations and, when not failing to sleep, listening to the radio. Distracting him from his pain were an array of songs, news reports, and radio shows imported from the rest of the continent, all fading into a haze. As he turned channels again, hearing Lleras Camargo's voice suddenly returned his senses to him.

“...olombia is a friend of freedom. We seek the common good of all, and hope to cooperate with all governments that think this way. For years, I have seen the United States in this light. Both of our countries were founded in a struggle against the colonial masters of Europe, with the goal of respecting the will of their people.” He turned himself around, attentive even through his coughs. He knew that some major discussions were about to happen when he was struck off; perhaps it was that?

A moment of silence was overshadowed by everything else. “But we are a proud people. Liberty means that nations are free, not simply to serve as puppets to larger nations, but to operate on their own ends. We should not be expected to respect other nations as they choose to occupy our lands. We do not respect the continued occupation of Korea by the Japanese, of Eastern Europe by the Germans, of Africa by the Italians and Iberians. And we do not respect the occupation of the San Andrés and Providen-”

The radio crackled as he turned it down, and then off, before burying his face in his hands, his mind clear once more. He had questioned the orders he'd been given for the past few weeks, but this? Lleras Camargo, from both what he'd read and seen, was the perfect man for Washington. Liberal, anti-extremist, pro-American. What would they be gaining from antagonizing him? Falling back into the bed, he dreaded returning to see through another round of negotiations.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.30.a: An ally, negotiated down to a foe.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.31.desc:
Resting in his chair, Lincoln Gordon sighed. There had been a real tension in the American embassy in the last few days, and his latest meeting had only underscored that fact. The negotiations in Colombia had not been going well, as had been repeatedly condemned  since the leaks a few days ago. Being in Brasília was enough to shield him from the fury that many American diplomats in Bogotá had faced, but the icy stares and backhanded comments of many Brazilian diplomats were more than enough. As the phone rang, he didn't expect much from what came beneath.

“Hello, this is Lincoln Gordon.”

“Mr. Gordon, this is Alberto Lleras Camargo,” replied the line, in accented yet fluent English. Gordon's eyes shot up. “The ambassadors on my end are totally silent, so I wanted to ask you. Why were we barred from reentering the Organization of American States?”

Gordon stuttered for a moment. “Well, I, um, am not the one to ask, I'm afraid. I know we talked a bit last month about managing discussions with Venezuela and Panama, but that was in line with the Brazilian government, and I can't discuss Washington's policy without further clarification.”

“The same line repeated by everybody else,” sighed Camargo, quickly enough not to be spoken over. “But I know you oppose this. You know that your government has betrayed their close ally and partner, and have hurt the aspirations of every Colombian on the ground. You just don't have the power to say so, do you?” Gordon struggled to speak, but his voice faltered in his mouth long enough for the line to die completely.

That had been an answer in itself, not that Gordon complained. Camargo was right, of course; he viewed the American decision as totally arbitrary. And what power did he have?
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.31.a: He just had to hope that the President wouldn't also turn his ire to Brazil.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.32.t: Portrait of a President on Fire
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.32.desc:
Taking one final look through his schedule, Henrique Lott smiled. He had a few documents still to read through, but his work was mostly finished, and his schedule tomorrow would be far more relaxed. The negotiations between Colombia and the United States had concluded, and he would be given a few days to remain with both delegations, offering his presence as an adjunct to Brazilian efforts. He took the document above, and immediately took care as soon as he realized the source.

FROM: PRESIDENT Alberto Lleras Camargo
TO: PRESIDENT and GENERAL Henrique Teixeira Lott

I want to thank you for the aid you have offered us. I have already made my gratitude to Brazil public, but I wanted to communicate more directly. Your career has been one of standing up for democracy against tyranny, and your pen is clearly as effective as your rifle. Thanks to you and the Itamaraty, Colombia is closer to being a free, democratic nation working alongside its Latin American brothers once more.

I have one final gift for you. I understand it is unusual, but I have chosen to dedicate a portrait to you. It should take a few more days to arrive in Brazil, but I chose to personally deliver it whilst thanking the staff of the Brazilian embassy in Bogotá. I apologize for how amateurish it is; being President, I have been unable to practice my skills to the level of Francisco de Goya. However, I hope that the message of peace and cooperation still comes, even through the poor quality of my art.“

Turning his eyes down, he noticed a small communique written from the embassy staff, describing the painting. It was nothing much - a standing portrait of him, done freehand, next to an olive tree - but was apparently well done. As he placed down the document, he laughed, took out his flask of whiskey, and began pouring it.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.32.a: A shame, he thought, that Edna would have to be the one to receive it.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.33.desc:
Standing impatiently, Lacerda's eyes jumped between the clock and then the phone. He was shortly to depart for an official meetingmorandum between the OFN and the Colombian government in Bogotá, but had one call first, pre-arranged in the small slot he still had free. As it rang, Lacerda jumped onto it.

“Hello, this is Lleras Camargo.” spoke the voice down the line. It wasn't, of course, it was a translator. He couldn't speak Spanish, and Camargo couldn't respond in Portuguese, so they arranged this as the solution. “I wanted to thank you for your support. We'd be in a far worse position without it.”

“It was no trouble, Alberto,” replied Lacerda, warmly. “We're both rational men, and in a world like this, that brings us together. I'm glad that we could come together for this.”

“Considering my opposition, it's nice to have a man who knows what's right. And a former journalist? I had my time writing articles to see my President reelected, but never went into it like you.”

“If only I could've been so kind about my leader!” Lacerda laughed, heartily. “Alas, when I started, it was Vargas or nothing.”

“Well, if I was in Brazil now, I definitely wouldn't be so critical of my President.” He sighed, as though releasing years of anguish, before continuing. “Decades after the memories of this war fade away, I know that Colombians will still repeat your name as our hero. You have it in you to be the hero for the rest of our continent.”

Lacerda offered his thanks, before being forced to end the call as a staffer burst in. Taking a moment to hover after hanging up, a smile kept creeping onto his face. Brazilian troops may not have been marching over Mt. Fuji or into the Volkshalle, but in his own way, he had helped to bring liberty to a dark corner of the world.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.Lleras.tt: Lleras is a skillful and pro-American diplomat, reducing our £political_power_texticon costs.
strings.COL_USA_negotiation.Pinilla.tt: Pinilla is a staunch nationalist, increasing our £political_power_texticon costs.
strings.COL_Volunteer.1.desc:
Good news come to the front today as the Colombian Government has announced its intentions to assemble and ship a battalion of volunteers to aid us in the Civil War, alongside several shipments of food rations and combat equipment of our own make that they received for their own conflict.

While the Colombian troops may not be many, they will be loyal to our cause and more importantly, battle-hardened from the decade of fighting which ravaged their homeland since the 50s. The news were well-received among the General Staff, with a few officers having warm reunions and the notion that, even if the Union may be dead, the connections our nation has built these past few decades still live on has brought hope to our soldiers.

We can only hope our other allies remember who stood by their side and join us in this national struggle.
strings.COL_News.3.desc:
The ongoing political crisis in Colombia has reached its finale as General Gustavo Rojas Pinilla, with the apparent unanimous support of the armed forces, has couped the government and formed a nationalist coalition following the passage of the PCC's Corporatist Constitution.

The General has indefinitely suspended elections and outlawed both of Colombia's traditional parties, forming the MAN in their stead with inspiration from Mexico's PRI. Surprisingly, internal opposition has already begun to collapse with leading figures fleeing the country for Iberia and many doubting their capabilities to organize a return.

During his inaugural speech, General Pinilla has promised to restore order to Colombia by any means necessary. With ultimatums sent to the rebel government within the day, it seems Colombia is heading towards war once more.
strings.COL_News.3.a: From the Athens of South America to Sparta.
strings.COL_News.4.desc:
It appears General Rojas Pinilla has finally lived up to expectations. Today, the General declared Martial Law and announced the creation of a Security Council composed of the nation's top military commanders, all of whom bear loyalty to Pinilla, to oversee the reunification of the nation.

The announcement came following the refusal of all insurgent groups to stand down. With the implementation of mandatory conscription and the ramping-up of its industry, it is clear that the Republic's primary goal in the following years will be reacquiring these territories by force.

While General Pinilla has stated the measures will be suspended after Reunification, many observers have expressed doubts. The announcement spurred protests in several cities but it appears the public mood is favorable, with many supportive of the Government's decisive action plan, for the time being that is.
strings.COL_News.1.desc:
The years since Laureano Gómez's death have been stormy for the Conservative regime in Colombia. However, the recent passing of the new constitution via the national constituent assembly and the pacification of rogue military elements seem to have stabilized the party and government, ending internal violence and allowing them to solidify their control over Bogotá and its surrounding territories.

Out of the crisis emerged a strengthened President Urdaneta, who has announced his intention to bring peace and unity to the country under the civilista banner. He has also made some favorable hints toward Germania, as was expected of a man of his character.
strings.COL_News.1.a: Will they be the force that decides?
strings.COL_News.2.desc:
The five year deadlock has finally ended in Colombia, with opposition forces ousting the Laureanist dictatorship and purging its elements.

The new government, a coalition of the Liberal Party and moderate Conservatives, has announced that elections have been scheduled to take place within the following months. Many expect the already weakened moderate Conservatives to be mere satellites to the Liberals.

The interim President Alberto Lleras Camargo has also announced overtures towards the OFN and a willingness to negotiate a peaceful end to the Colombian Conflict.
strings.COL_News.2.a: Democracy may have been returned to Colombia, but is it enough to prevent a civil war?
strings.COL_News.5.t: {get_newspaper_header}The First Elections of the National Front
strings.COL_News.5.desc:
The 1964 Colombian elections, scheduled by the interim National Front government following the recent ousting of the Laureanist Government, have concluded today with the victory of the Interim President of Colombia Alberto Lleras Camargo of the Liberal Party.

Lleras Camargo has promised an ambitious reformist agenda, which includes everything from decentralization by creating new forms of local governance to the promotion of a new industrial base for the reconstruction of the country, while including plans for labor, bank and healthcare reform. The new President is also notably interested in restoring trade and diplomatic relations with the United States.

The Conservative Party, which did not nominate a candidate in the election, has recognized the result of the election and promised to cooperate with the Liberals and help bring forth a new dawn for the country.
strings.COL_News.5.a: And so Colombians dare to hope once more.
strings.COL_News.6.desc:
Facilitated by Brazil, the United States and Colombia have begun a series of talks aiming to restore amicable ties. Relations broke down in the mid-50s following nationalizations of American firms under the previous, Germanophilic Laureanist government, with Washington recalling its ambassador in protest.

The negotiations could prove pivotal for the new Colombian government, which is seeking international support and internal legitimacy to resolve La Violencia, an ongoing low-level civil war. Nevertheless, Bogotá will be hard-pressed to settle issues like German relations, the fate of the nationalized businesses, and the return of the U.S.-occupied island of San Andrés without domestic backlash.
strings.COL_News.8.desc:
In what seems to be the best outcome, the negotiations between the United States and the Republic of Colombia have concluded with a nigh-perfect agreement between the parties involved, a movement that, after the Civil War, seems to return the time to the fresh start that the Mallarino-Bidlack Treaty signified in 1854.

In the final resolution, the United States and Colombia have agreed to cooperate in commercial affairs, reintegrating Colombia to the inter-American system of diplomacy and committing to not interfere or significantly hinder the other's interests, settling the bases for effective normalization and the return of permanent diplomatic missions to Washington DC and Bogotá respectively.

Optimism has risen as the implementation of the agreements moves forward and a historically friendly relation blooms after decades in the shadows.
strings.COL_News.7.t: {get_newspaper_header}Colombia and the United States Agree on the Fundamentals
strings.COL_News.7.desc:
An agreement has been reached in the aftermath of the negotiations between the governments of the United States of America and the Republic of Colombia, although it seems that despite the efforts from both sides to achieve common goals, the recent wounds in bilateral relationships and the tensions of the past decade have hindered the opportunity of full reconciliation.

The basis of this attempt at reconciliation began when the change in administration in Colombia turned more favorable to the United States and the diplomatic climate after the civil war became adequate enough to push for a solution, albeit an underwhelming one for the time being.

For now, as both governments have resolved to stand up from the dialogue table, no further conditions will be agreed on or discussed. However, many see this move as positive for the position of democracy and stability in the region.
strings.COL_News.9.desc:
Talks concluded successfully between Bogotá and Washington today, with both thanking Brazil for facilitating the meetings. Relations between the two broke down in the mid-50s following nationalizations of American firms under the previous, Germanophilic Laureanist government. The return to amicable ties marks a triumph for the new Colombian government, with the U.S. embassy soon to be re-established.

The agreement is expected to upend the dynamics of La Violencia, the civil conflict that has plagued Colombia for years. The invigorated central government anticipates greater access to American arms, while Supreme Commander Salcedo of the Colombian Revolutionary Union rebels has decried the reconciliation as “a betrayal of the will of the Colombian people.”
strings.COL_News.10.desc:
Talks between the U.S. and the Bogotá government in Colombia have broken down, with each side accusing the other of obstinance. Brazilian officials, who had facilitated the negotiations, expressed disappointment that the two former partners were unable to “overcome the legacy of the Laureanist era” and achieve reconciliation.

Other parties in La Violencia, Colombia's long-running civil conflict, are overjoyed. Supreme Commander Salcedo of the Colombian Revolutionary Union rebels issued a statement that “the North Americans have recognized the folly of engaging an illegitimate government against the wishes of the Colombian people.” Alzate of New Granada attacked Bogotá's “willingness to sell our nation to foreign foes, and incompetence at doing even that.”
strings.COL_News.10.a: A decade's damage is not easily set aside.
strings.COL_News.11.desc:
Outstanding news from Colombia today as the FN Government has announced the success of negotiations for the peaceful reunification of the Revolutionary Front with the Republic.

The Lleras government has promised amnesty for many within the Front and permitted elements to join the Colombian Armed Forces. Politically, the move guarantees a left-ward shift in the Liberal party and a the revival of Gaitanist policies within the party mainstream.

The popular reaction to the announcement has been very positive, especially from the OFN who has promised to help the new coalition rebuild. Many have likened this outcome to a new Marching Revolution like that of President Pumarejo in the 30s.

Tensions with the right of the political spectrum have risen drastically as a result, though few expect New Granada could pose a threat to this new union.
strings.COL_News.11.a: The effect of respect for mutual rights
strings.COL_News.12.desc:
Shocking news have emerged from Colombia today as a new contender in La Violencia appeared. The Second Patriotic Army, capitalized on the weakness of the Bogotá Government and seized the northern city of Barranquilla and much of the North.

The Second Patriotic Army is comprised of the remaining forces loyal to the Laureanist which were ousted from power in 1962. The SPA's leadership is staffed by pro-German cadres, with one of the SPA's key advisors being rumoured to have worked with the Abwehr and many others bearing ties to the German community.

Due to the Government's unpopularily in a region known as “Colombia's festering wound”, the growing momentum of the SPA should not come as a surprise.
strings.COL_News.13.desc:
The armed peace in which Colombians have lived since a ceasefire was agreed in 1956 has ended as the three struggling factions, the Central Government, the Colombian Revolutionary Union, and New Granada have resumed their war operations following the escalation of the brutal skirmishes for control of northern Colombia. The rise of the Second Patriotic Army and their sudden takeover of the Atlántico department has only further destabilized the region.

What is to become of Colombia now is not known, but with the warring factions throwing peace out of the window motivated by hatred, desperation, and greed, the country has been violently returned to the bloodshed of the 50s. And as the bodies begin to accumulate in the mountains, streets, and jungles, it might come the day when people look back at La Violencia as a better time, as none is safe from the looming threat of death and the outreach of armies and militias across the scorched land.
strings.COL_News.13.a: A peaceful solution always seemed impossible to begin with.
strings.COL_News.14.t: {get_newspaper_header}Government Victory in the Colombian Civil War
strings.COL_News.14.desc:
The Colombian Liberal Party has come a long way since the start of the decade. Where it was once expected to fade into the long and troubled history of Colombian politics, it has miraculously recovered against the exhausted conservatives and achieved the impossible: restoring the rule of law and ending the Violencia by reclaiming Colombia from all opposition through military action.

Under President Lleras Camargo, the government has promised to restore democracy and normalcy via reforms while also pledging to protect those values abroad. By doing so, they hope to ensure that the lessons of the Colombian Civil War are understood and that the tragedy may never repeat.
strings.COL_News.15.t: {get_newspaper_header}Government Victory in the Colombian Civil War
strings.COL_News.15.desc:
Gustavo Rojas Pinilla, nicknamed the “Caesar of the Andes” by his soldiers, has crossed the Rubicon and ended the Violencia after seizing power from the nation's old government elites and crushing all opposing factions on the battlefield. While some insurgents have refused to give up the fight, the general has vindicated his failed campaigns in '56 and '57; his promises of stability and social justice have swayed the masses.

While emphasising Colombian independence from foreign influence, the Generalissimo has not forgotten those who stood at his side, such as the Mexican ambassador at his victory speech, implying plans for a closer relationship with their northern neighbor.
strings.COL_News.15.a: Order has been restored to the Andes.
strings.COL_News.16.t: {get_newspaper_header}Government Victory in the Colombian Civil War
strings.COL_News.16.desc:
Colombia's political hegemon, the Conservative Party, has persevered over its opposition once again. Its sole leader, Roberto Urdaneta, the viceroy to Laureano Gómez, announced a final victory over the Republic's enemies, reversing the government's losses from the previous years of turmoil and bloodshed.

Although the party has maintained its status as the political hegemon of Colombia and preserved its course, much remains uncertain for the party. There is no clear answer as to whether victory will reshuffle the government or if Urdaneta's continuity is out of question. Regardless, the country's radical transformation into a dictatorship of tradition, powered by a growing industry, is becoming more evident to international observers.
strings.COL_News.17.desc:
The URC's triumph over the myriad opposing forces in Colombia's long-running civil war was celebrated today with a march down Bogotá's cobblestoned streets. Once rag-tag revolutionary troops displayed discipline as residents of the city assembled to greet them with music and steaming bowls of changua and ajiaco.

The parade culminated in the Plaza de Bolívar, where, framed by mountaintops and the Palace of Justice, Supreme Commander Salcedo announced that he would be stepping down in three months' time and that a People's Cabildo would then administer free elections. He hailed the sacrifices of his troops, the Colombian people, and that of Gaitán, whose assasination Salcedo claimed was avenged at last.
strings.COL_News.17.a: The idealists have won the war, can they win the peace?
strings.COL_News.18.t: {get_newspaper_header}New Granada Wins the Colombian Civil War
strings.COL_News.18.desc:
The Colombian Civil War has finally come to an end today as the New Granadan government led by “Duce” Gilberto Alzate Avendaño declared victory earlier this morning. The Cali-based government has been supported by the Italian Empire since the beginning of the conflict, and the Italian government has issued their congratulations to Avendaño.

At his address today, Avendaño declared that “the New Granadan State will bring new and old glories” to the Colombian people. Avendaño's government has already begun to implement corporatist policies inspired by Italy and Japan's own policies.

The big tent coalition of other far-right parties seems to be a fragile one, with political disagreements already flaring up over issues of policy, including minor ones such as the changing of the country's name to New Granada.
strings.COL_News.18.b: They'll collapse in a week... surely?
strings.COL_News.18.c: An old name breathed new life.
strings.COL_News.19.t: {get_newspaper_header}Second Patriotic Army Victory in the Colombian Civil War!
strings.COL_News.19.desc:
Troubling news comes from Colombia as the dust settles from the civil war with the Second Patriotic Army as victor. Composed of the PCC's most far-right cliques, the Laureanists, led by Alfonso Uribe Misas, and José Camacho Carreño's Nacional-Americanista Movement, the SPA victory represents a worrying departure from the previous governments compromise politics.

More troubling than their totalitarian politics and unrepentant germanophilia, the new government inherits a nation devastated by two decades of Civil War. The prospects for reconstruction and the government's ability to stabilize the country, in light of the continued insurgencies and political infighting, are grim.
strings.COL_News.20.desc:
Important news from Colombia today as President Roberto Urdaneta has announced his retirement. Urdaneta will be remembered for leading the PCC ever since the death of its primarch, Laureano Eleuterio Gómez, during the late 50s and for presiding over the reunification of the country.

The announcement has been received positively, primarily due to his decision to confirm Gómez's son, Álvaro as the new President. Álvaro is known for his reputation as a more moderate figure, especially in comparison to the arch-conservative reputation of his father. Notably he is also less enthusiastic about the PCC's overtures to Germania, with many expecting him to work towards reversing such developments during his term.

Álvaro's leadership is likely to bring moderation to the PCC's rhetoric. Though it is undeniable it will remain unchallengeable.
strings.COL_News.20.a: May he bring peace and stability to his father's empire.
strings.COL_News.20.b: How moderate can a monster's prodigy really be?
strings.COL_News.20.c: He best not forget who won him the Civil War.
strings.COL_News.21A.desc:
President Álvaro Gómez Hurtado successfully passed his landmark reform package through the Colombian Senate earlier today, hailing the legislative achievement as “clearing the way for new development.” Political observers had been skeptical that the bill would pass, as multiple Senate hardliners, many of whom had life-tenure in the Senate, had expressed their dissatisfaction with the proposal. Those doubts appear to have been overstated, as the party expressed their broad support for the bill and it passed well above the threshold of success.

The new reform package has permitted local elections and restored the position of the Vice Presidency. The bill also mandated a minimum wage to address poverty while maintaining Catholicism as the state religion, calling on all Colombians to renew their faith and love for their fellow man in the wake of the brutal civil war.
strings.COL_News.21A.a: With open hands and faithful hearts.
strings.COL_News.21B.desc:
Colombian President Álvero Gómez's proposed reforms have failed following fierce opposition from the Senate. Coming to power with the Conservative party, Gómez's proposed reforms attempted to democratize and streamline the central bureaucratic apparatus, with a reintroduction of the Vice President and local elections being some of the proposed reforms.

With the death of the reforms, Gómez faces a tight battle to negotiate with hardliners within his party, with some observers speculating that he may need to compromise on Cabinet positions or on critical policy decisions. As many of his political opponents are reaching mandatory retirement age, Gómez may be hoping to wait for a more advantageous political position to advance his reforms.
strings.COL_News.22.desc:
With Lozano and Pabón failing to reach a successful compromise for the leadership of Colombia, the constitutional majority in the Constituent Assembly favored Elías Salazar García, the head of the NCL, Colombia's sole legal trade union since 1956 as the new minister of government. 

A friend of General Pinilla, they first became acquainted in Cali during Salazar García's time as an agitator. Since then, through infusing Colombian nationalism with the worker's movement, he made himself the main labor organizer in the western regions. As he fled alongside loyalists during La Violencia, he became the general's favorite in dealing with labor relations. Known for a tendency of erratic actions and having expressed a desire to dissolve the CED, combined with a lack of qualms against violence, many business owners are making exit plans as he comes to power.
strings.COL_News.23.desc:
Former Colombian leader, Gustavo Rojas Pinilla, was announced dead after an alleged air accident thirty miles north of Bogotá. Rumor has it that Pinilla, fearing a loss of power after growing conflicts between the general and minister Salazar García over low export prices, was allegedly heading to exile in Mexico before the plane had crashed. At the accident, Salazar García offered no comment on the matter. The government has yet to issue a statement on if they believe foul play was involved.

Hours after the death of Gustavo Rojas Pinllia, a proclamation announcing the Authentic Socialist Alliance as the sole ruling party was made official, coupled with the nomination of Salazar for the role of inteurim, and most likely perpetual president.
strings.COL_News.23.a: Has luck never smiled at Colombia?
strings.COL_News.24.t: {get_newspaper_header}The National Constituent Assembly is Convened in Colombia
strings.COL_News.24.desc:
Following Colombia's recent victory in its civil conflict, General Pinilla has convened the National Constituent Assembly as promised and through which begins a transference of the Security Council's emergency power back to civilian control. Initially intended to be summoned before the war, it has been delayed until present due to the declaration of a state of siege that rendered control to Pinilla's council.

Seeing a return to normalcy for the most part, the assembly is set to revise many laws, including the constitution, in the following meeting. More importantly, it is during this time that Pinilla's successor shall be chosen by the National Assembly representatives, marking a return of democratic rule.
strings.COL_News.24.a: Can't make an omelette without cracking some eggs.
strings.COL_News.25.desc:
The military rule in Colombia comes to an end as General Pinilla signs the new constitution under popular vote in the assembly, with Juan Lozano y Lozano chosen as the new minister of government, prompting an immediate transition of power as promised before by the general. As the leader of the restored Patriotic National Economic Action, or APEN for short, Lozano y Lozano had managed to become a darling for businessmen and liberal intellectuals alike, and during La Violencia, acted instrumentally in Pinilla's power brokering.

Chosen from a compromise with Lucio Pabón, Lozano y Lozano has earned a poor reputation as a mouthpiece for corporate backers such as Julio Mario Santo Domingo.
