However, given his experience in wrestling the CED before, though a rather controversial candidate, he may just be able to bring about a promise of national prosperity unheard of for decades.
strings.COL_News.26.desc:
The assembly has made its will clear as voting for the new constitution ends, with General Pinilla accepting the confidence vote and appointing Lucio Pabón as minister of government. As leader of the National Action Movement, sponsored primarily by the traditional establishment, Pabón won Pinilla's trust during La Violencia through his unusual economic acumen, notably for drafting the recovery initiative known as the “Three-Year Plan,” likely to be soon implemented as he shall assume office.

Behind the scenes, Pabón's appointment was tenuously kept through compromises with Juan Lozano y Lozano, who agreed to break the assembly's gridlock in exchange for a secondary administrative role over the next four years. Though expected, many insiders note this uneasy alliance may soon fall apart with Elías Salazar out of the picture.
strings.COL_News.26.a: A house of cards standing on stilts.
strings.COL_News.27.t: {get_newspaper_header}Carlos Lleras Restrepo Elected New President of Colombia“ #
strings.COL_News.27.desc:
The Colombian Liberal Party has declared victory after running an unopposed contest in the 1968 legislative elections. Following the collapse of the Conservative Party's leadership, the Liberal Party was the sole legal party standing in the election. After a fierce leadership struggle, Carlos Lleras Restrepo, the former leader of the dissident caucus, will replace his distant cousin Alberto Lleras as the President. The new President cheerfully addressed his supporters following the announcement of his victory, promising to maintain peace in Colombia and provide relief to regions and peoples devastated by the recent civil war, with the hope of restoring democracy in Colombia's near future.

Outside observers express doubt in President Lleras's policy direction, believing that he will be unable to maintain peace without increasing police powers and runs a risk of inflation due to his monetary policy, but the President was able to secure the support of the Liberal Party, and he hopes to similarly win the support of his people.
strings.COL_News.27.a: Can the white dove carry a red rose?
strings.COL_News.28.t: {get_newspaper_header}Hernando Durán Dussán Elected New President of Colombia
strings.COL_News.28.desc:
The 1968 Colombian legislative elections have finally concluded to find a surprising result. While the Liberal Party was expected to secure an overwhelming victory due to conservative disarray, many independent legislators secured seats in the Constituent Assembly. The Assembly has named Hernando Durán Dussán, once exiled from Colombia due to his political activism, as the new President of Colombia.

The President stated that he would fulfill a democratic mandate for Colombia, ending political persecution, and securing the return of those who were exiled for political purposes. He also promised a new economic platform, reducing the state's role in industrialization and dismantling corporatist structures. Opponents decry his economic platform, stating it will increase poverty and inequality, but the President was undeterred, stating that political freedom requires economic freedom.
strings.COL_News.28.a: Liberate the mind, liberate the market, and you liberate the people.
strings.COL_News.29.desc:
Following “an exhaustion of political capital”, President Alberto Lleras Camargo has informed the country this morning of his intention to step down. Longtime leader of the Liberal party and the man credited with signing the Havana Peace Accords with the insurgents of the Colombian Revolutionary Union, Lleras has announced that the functions of the presidency will be held by Julio César Turbay, standing president of the Senate, until elections can be organized in the coming months.

Lleras' announcement comes as little surprise, as plans for a transition to full democratic rule were outlined at the signing of the peace accords. Contrary to the predictions of those who believed Liberal rule would lead to anarchy, this development seems to reveal the surprisingly rapid stabilization of Colombian institutions and political life.
strings.COL_News.29.c: One president or another, Colombia remains bound by degeneracy.
strings.COL_News.67.desc:
Following a worsening conflict between Lucio Pabón and Juan Lozano y Lozano, culminating in a series of contradictory messages turning into complete silence over the past week, the details of what has now been dubbed the “July Conspiracy” have come to light. The most direct result of the conspiracy has been the resignation of Pabón from all government positions and the dissolution of his National Action Movement, leaving APEN to head the Colombian government on its own.

With these events, it seems that APEN and business leaders have succeeded in pressuring Pinilla into allowing them to establish a new oligarchy, with industry leaders playing an outsized role in the reshaping of the regime. It is now expected that the reforms already promulgated during the reconstruction process will pick up steam, and that the growing caste of industrialists will further expand its operations.
strings.COL_News.67.b: He has succumbed to the grip of international finance.
strings.COL_News.68.desc:
The brewing political crisis in Colombia came to a head this week, following a worsening conflict between Lucio Pabón and Juan Lozano y Lozano and growing fears of a government collapse. In a hastily-organized press conference, Pabón had announced the shocking news of Lozano's arrest and the outlawing of his APEN party, for attempting to stage a coup against the government.

While it seems that the business magnates known to be connected to APEN have so far escaped any direct consequences, the ousting of their front party likely means that a second three-year-plan is in order, and that it will come at the expense of their political power. The free-market reforms already promulgated by the government during the reconstruction process have not currently been repealed, but few expect them to pick up further steam now.
strings.COL_News.68.a: It seems that Colombia needs a steady hand.
strings.COL_News.68.b: Their petty squabbles will doom them.
strings.COL_News.68.c: At least there wasn't a civil war this time...
strings.COL_News.69.desc:
Following weeks of upheaval from the Oil Crisis, the National Confederation of Labors have launched a nationwide strike under interim leader Tulio Cuevas Romero. Colombia, already having been weakened from the Oil Crisis, is now seemingly paralyzed as the nation comes to a halt. The government under Pinilla has ordered police and armed forces into the streets to end these strikes and arrest any agitators.

Questions surround the involvement of former union leader Salazar García as well as Pinillas current position as his government is weakening as these crises continue.
strings.COL_News.69.a: Another nail in the Colombian coffin.
strings.COL_News.70.t: {get_newspaper_header}Elías Salazar García Executed in Army Putsch
strings.COL_News.70.desc:
Following weeks of paralyzing strikes and increasingly severe conflicts within the government of Colombia, reports indicate that the army has finally decided to intervene. This morning, the Presidential Guard and the 13th Brigade marched on the national capitol, closing the restored congress of the republic.

Any lingering doubts about the authority behind the lockdown were dispelled by a broadcast of General Pinilla in the CATAM airbase, where he denounced the strikers as Salazar's lackeys, intent on toppling the republic and its government. He has announced the restoration of the Security Council, the dissolution of the CNT, and the death of Salazar, who many believe was summarily executed by members of the F2 department in his own home.
strings.COL_News.70.a: The Caesar of the Andes, true to his name.
strings.COL_News.70.b: Once more the folly of National Syndicalism is proven.
strings.COL_News.30.t: {get_newspaper_header}The Revolutionary Cabildo of Colombia is Inaugurated
strings.COL_News.30.desc:
Commander-in-chief of the Revolutionary Armed Forces and interim head of state of Colombia Guadalupe Salcedo Unda has stepped down from his position.

In accordance with the Basic Law, the socialist revolutionaries now ruling Colombia have moved one step closer to creating a formal governance structure by declaring the establishment of a Revolutionary Cabildo, or governing council.

Elections for the legislature and constituent assembly are to begin soon. During the next year, representatives from all of Colombia will meet in Bogotá to discuss the articles of the Union's constitution and hammer out the legal framework of the Republic.
strings.COL_News.31.desc:
The elections to the Revolutionary Cabildo of Colombia have returned a result—that the adherents of the late caudillo Jorge Eliécer Gaitán will have won the majority in both the constituent assembly and the Cabildo.

The Gaitanistas of the MRL are expected to continue the late Caudillo's grand vision for a fair republic driven by ideals of mutual respect and social justice. While accusations of voter suppression and electoral fraud may have soured the mood in the Capital, it seems much of the population is still celebrating, which should be no surprise with to the Caudillo's popularity.

While the OAS has refused to comment on the allegations, OFN delegations across Bogotá have joined in the celebrations and many expect this victory to represent the practical accession of a new member to the grand alliance of the free world.
strings.COL_News.31.a: Can they live up his legacy?
strings.COL_News.32.desc:
Church bells ring out throughout Colombia as the elections for the first constituent assembly and Cabildo yield their result, a victory for the Frente Unido del Pueblo, a coalition of socialist parties which refused to submit to the MRL.

The Coalition, led by Camilo Torres's Christian Socialists, has promised to uphold democratic practices and ensure the church an active role in the preservation of revolutionary triumphs and protocols through the doctrine of 'efficient love'.

While many on the right denounced his socialist tendencies as a perversion of Catholic ideals, Torres' leadership has been widely endorsed across the country, especially since the opposition had been hit by allegations of voter suppression and electoral fraud.
strings.COL_News.34.desc:
Shocking news from Colombia today as Communist paramilitaries have stormed the Revolutionary Cabildo and removed the provisional government from power.

Tensions between the Communist Party and the Government had been running high ever since the decision to ban them from the upcoming elections and it seems that the recent reports of voter suppression and electoral fraud in multiple regions were the last straw for their cooperation.

In his inaugural speech, the new president, Viera White, has promised to free the Colombian proletariat from its chains and restore a free and democratic Colombia. Furthermore, the President denounced the United States and OAS for ignoring the so-called clear signs of undemocratic practices in the elections.
strings.COL_News.33.desc:
Alarm in Bogotá as elections to the Revolutionary Cabildo and constituent assembly have resulted in total gridlock, with no faction having enough representatives even to command a decisive plurality. The new assemblies, having sat down, are increasingly descending into acrimony.

Hostile intra-fraction rhetoric has destabilised the coalition. The prior rivalry between Gaitanistas and Communists has been inflamed, and has led to groups of supporters of both factions fighting in the streets of Bogotá and other major cities.

It is commonly feared that the upcoming result, whatever it is, may result in tragedy for the young revolutionary republic.
strings.COL_News.35.desc:
It seems tensions in the new Republic of Colombia have once more boiled over as the military, led by Rafael Navas Pardo has violently couped the government and established a “temporary” dictatorship to restore order.

Citing undemocratic practices and and the empowering of dangerous radicals as the reasons for the coup, many believe the military's distrust of socialists and communists as the true reason for the coup. Clashes have taken place around the country but resistance efforts struggle to match the might of the organized military response.

The leader of the new Junta is the well-known marshal of the FR's Rebel forces during the war, a Pro-Gaitanist figure with a reputation for discipline, General Navas has promised a return to democracy following a brief decommunization period and renewed international ties.
strings.COL_News.35.b: Nothing more democratic than a military dictatorship.
strings.COL_News.36A.t: {get_newspaper_header}Alfonso López Michelsen Declares State of Siege
strings.COL_News.36A.desc:
It seems that the last few years were built on a false hope. In the wake of a major political crisis, and with claims of clientelism and corruption spreading across Colombia, many observers feared that a wave of protests would erupt. These have been disproven, but only with President Alfonso López Michelsen announcing the implementation of martial law, and the adoption of emergency powers.

The move, which has suspended the rights to protest, the People's Cabildo of the Republic and has implemented a curfew from 8:00PM, has been vociferously attacked in what channels still survive by the Liberal Revolutionary Movement and the National Workers' Confederation, labelling these moves as tantamount to a coup. Surprisingly, Colombia's partners have not issued a statement in response, but the army's presence on the streets and the mass arrests of political dissidents proves one thing:
strings.COL_News.36A.a: Once more, the dream of Gaitán lies dead.
strings.COL_News.36B.desc:
Once again, the balance of power shifts in Colombia. The short-lived government of military junta of General Rafael Navas Pardo has announced the end of the reconstruction period and the appointment of Alfonso López Michelsen as President, with power returning to a greatly weakened People's Cabildo, alongside the end to emergency measures such as the curfew system.

Whilst supported by many surviving political parties, Michelsen remains a controversial figure, and his presidency threatens to inflame tensions and further divide the country. The allegations of corruption and his strong ties to the military as well as endorsement by the old Liberal Party paint a grim picture during times of an already growing insurgency, with the whereabouts of most opposition leaders still uncertain.
strings.COL_News.36B.a: Those who make peaceful revolution impossible...
strings.COL_News.37.t: {get_newspaper_header}Gilberto Vieira White Confirmed in 11th Congress of the Colombian Communist Party
strings.COL_News.37.desc:
Following the takeover of the Colombian Revolutionary Union and a purge against the army, the 11th Congress of the Colombian Communist Party has been convened, marking the first time the party has been in power. During the congress, party delegates drafted a new constitution and gave a vote of confidence to the Standing General Secretary and Chairman of the Central Executive Committee of the Party, Gilberto Vieira White, who will remain in both positions. White also assumed the presidency of the newly founded Council of Ministers of the People's Republic, making him the de facto leader of the country.

Some experts have compared the process to the congresses of the Communist Party of the now-dead Soviet Union, with the Colombian Communist Party acting as a highly centralized and “bolshevized” organization. White, the General-Secretary since 1947, shall be the man to steward Communism in Colombia.
strings.COL_News.37.c: Do all socialists have really long titles?
strings.COL_News.38.t: {get_newspaper_header}Nicolás Buenaventura Alder Elected in 11th Congress of the Colombian Communist Party
strings.COL_News.38.desc:
Following the Colombian Communist Party's takeover of the People Cabildo and a subsequent purge against the army, the Colombian Communist Party holds its 11th Party Congress, and its first as a ruling party. In the congress, party delegates drafted a new constitution and, in a surprising course of action, voted for Nicolás Buenaventura Alder to become the new party secretary and Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the People's Republic.

Buenaventura has been a lifelong activist and has come to lead the left wing of the party. Buenaventura stated that he would pursue a “vigorous Leninst course of action to ensure economic prosperity on behalf of the workers, to bring the victory of Communism from Colombia to the entire region.” The new General-Secretary also pledged to follow his predecessor's path in ridding Colombia of the scourge of fascism.
strings.COL_News.39A.t: {get_newspaper_header}Antonio García Nossa wins the Colombian Elections of 1970
strings.COL_News.39A.desc:
Celebrations can be heard all across Bogotá today as the unified leftist coalition of the Patriotic Union stands victorious in the highly contested popular elections, shattering most expectations.

Running on a Gaitánist platform, newly elected leader Antonio García Nossa, a former economic advisor of the late caudillo Jorge Eliécer Gaitán's cabinet, takes charge of the country at the closure of a chaotic decade, and has already been quoted reiterating his commitment to bold social and land reforms.

Despite eager expectations that his victory will finally bring relief after the horrors of La Violencia, some international observers offered a more measured response, fearing the new policies might cause further instability by sparking a reaction from the country's large conservative opposition.
strings.COL_News.39A.a: A ray of hope in a sea of turmoil.
strings.COL_News.39B.t: {get_newspaper_header}Antonio García Nossa Wins the 1970 Extraordinary Elections
strings.COL_News.39B.desc:
A surprising new face appears in Bogotá as socialist candidate Antonio García Nossa emerges as the relatively undisputed winner of the emergency elections held by the People's Cabildo, taking the place of his predecessor Alfonso López Michelsen. The extraordinary process was initiated by a popular motion after the result of recent investigations led many to question the legitimacy of the previous election.

At the helm of the Colombian Socialist Movement, international observers wonder how the leader of the eclectic Gaitánist coalition, which also includes former members of the Caribbean Legion and the late caudillo's daughter Gloria Gaitán, will prove up to the task as the republic enters the new decade. With the situation slowly returning to normal, many hope that this victory will finally steer the fragile republic into a more humane direction.
strings.COL_News.40A.desc:
Michelsen's legacy has been secured. Although he has been swamped by poor relations with his domestic opposition, investigations into his personal conduct and clientelism, the President has maintained a sizable base of support among the Colombian electorate. Some feared that ongoing investigations would jeopardise his long-term ambitions, but as he stands triumphant, it is clear that they didn't prevent his reelection.

While the accusations of fraud relating to the election have been rejected by Colombia's electoral authority, this has done little to quell the unrest with protests announced in the capital and other major cities. Irregardless, these results have affirmed the status of the Liberal Revolutionary Movement as inheritors to Gaitán's legacy, but with rising pressures, only time will tell whether their vision for the country will last.
strings.COL_News.40A.a: Libertad y Orden, upheld within Bogotá.
strings.COL_News.40B.t: {get_newspaper_header}Alfonso López Michelsen Wins the 1970 Extraordinary Elections
strings.COL_News.40B.desc:
Following the resignation of President Camilo Torres Restrepo, the People's Cabildo held new elections. With the collapse of Restrepo's United People's Front due to a rift between the former president's associates, Alfonso López Michelsen and his Liberal Revolutionary Front have secured victory with a sizable majority.

Alfonso López Michelsen, also known as “el Pollo,” was a notable popular figure sidelined by President Restrepo after he took office.. With his popularity, some have said that this victory was deferred, and that he should have been President in 1968. Michelsen, with his mandate secured, thanked his supporters and pledged to bring his ideals into reality.
strings.COL_News.41.desc:
The end of La Violencia brought about a new order in the Athens of South America yet now doubts arise about its longevity due to the death of El Duce, Gilberto Alzate Avendaño, following a long fight with cancer, mere months after the Civil War ended. Shortly following the announcement of Avendaño's death, New Granada's Grand Council of Fascism has announced that it will assume emergency powers to elect a new Duce.

The Grand Council also announced the release of an official testament of the late leader and the publishing of his memoirs within the upcoming days.

In an interesting twist, the recent meetings of the Grand Council show an empowered nationalist wing and with the ANP allying itself with much of the old Conservative establishment of the Republic, many now wonder what will become of the Duce's plans to bring Fascism to Colombia.
strings.COL_News.41.a: Even in death we may yet live on.
strings.COL_News.42.desc:
Shocking news from Bogotá as the ANP has announced that an attempted coup by the Oligarchs of the Supreme Economic Council has been violently crushed. It appears the party's position as hegemon of Colombia continues to be unchallengeable

Alongside the expected news of purges among the ranks of capitalists and oligarchs alike, the government has come forward to announce the election of a new Duce, Augusto Ramírez Moreno, who had been serving as Interim Leader since the Alzate died.

Moreno is known for being a founding member of Los Leopardos, the group which inspired Alzate however Moreno appears to be hold more moderate views and is known for being part of the party's Nationalist Caucus. Time will tell what his rule will mean for New Granada.
strings.COL_News.42.a: A colossus's unfettered or rotting from the inside?
strings.COL_News.42.f: Perhaps this could be played to our advantage...
strings.COL_News.43.desc:
In New Granada, an organization known as the Asociación Nacional de Industriales de Colombia, composed of the nation's leading capitalists and industrialists, has made a surprising putsch. This coup d'etat has expelled the ANP from power, giving the business council full control over the state.

At the head of ANDI is Diego Garcés Giraldo, the creator of the Supreme Economic Council, the development authority responsible for New Granada's massive economic growth. He succeeds the recently assassinated Julio Mario Santo Domingo which promised a return to democracy and liberalization.

Only time will tell if the new administration will adheer to his promises or if its purpose is simply strengthening Colombia's latest pack of overlords.
strings.COL_News.43.a: Rekindled liberty or just a facade?
strings.COL_News.43.b: An opening is all we need.
strings.COL_News.44.desc:
Instability continues to rock Colombia as Augusto's Ramírez Moreno's government has survived a coup attempt from the party's hardline wing, led by Silvio Villegas, a close friend of Ramírez, which represented the bastion of Fascism within the ANP. With its members now purged, it appears Fascism in Colombia is its the way out.

In equally surprising news, in the days following the coup attempt, Moreno has announced a wide range of government reforms, the plans of which likely triggered the coup. Most important among these reforms is the institution of a new Constitution modeled on the Republic's 1886 Constitution which officially names the new state “The National Republic of Colombia”.

The newly declared President has promised to uphold Alzate's ideals while also promising the new Republic be a truly national one.
strings.COL_News.44.b: All is fair in love and politics.
strings.COL_News.44.c: The best outcome we could have hoped for.
strings.COL_News.44.d: Less black but a Black Spot on the Continent nonetheless.
strings.COL_News.44.f: And so adiós it is to our old partner.
strings.COL_News.45.desc:
More news out of New Granada today as Augusto Ramírez Moreno, leader of the nation and successor to Avendaño, has been removed from government by what some experts are calling an “internal party coup”. Silvio Villegas, previously the Executive Secretary of the Party, has now been sworn in as president.

This change of leadership has come after harsh internal criticism of Moreno by opposing parties. A vote of no confidence was unexpectedly passed by a slim majority, leading to Villegas' ascension to the presidency.

Villegas is a hardliner in the New Granadan system, especially when compared to Moreno. In his inauguration speech he vowed to “uphold the Fascist ideals of our country in thought and deed.” He then pledged to transform New Granada into a fully Fascist country, despite the many challenges and obstacles in its, and his, future.
strings.COL_News.45.a: I thought the point of Fascism was to not get voted out?
strings.COL_News.46.t: {get_newspaper_header}Old Guard Conservatives Coup Government in Colombia
strings.COL_News.46.desc:
Developments out of Colombia continue to surprise, as it appears that a coalition of moderate generals and aristocrats have couped the government. Earlier today, the new government has confirmed that Archbishop Raúl Zambrano Camader will lead a temporary national unity government, sheparding the country's recovery from La Violencia.

The coalition' appear shaky however and concerns rise over the new government's collaboration with the fascist ANP, from which its entire leadership seems to originate. It appears Colombia will be looking to its past for inspiration and unsurprisingly to the Iberian Peninsula, as the new government is largely composed of Hispanophiles.

No information has been given in regards to a return to civilian governance.
strings.COL_News.47.t: {get_newspaper_header}Fernando Londoño y Londoño is Appointed as Interim Leader
strings.COL_News.47.desc:
When Colombian President Silvio Villegas announced his intent to nationalize all industries represented in the Supreme Economic Council, he had kicked off months of economic turmoil and political uproar. This crisis appears to have been culminated with a vote of no confidence against Villegas, ousting him from power, but leaving no clear successor in his wake.

In order to end the deadlock, the party had voted to elect Fernando Londoño y Lodoño, the former Minister of Propaganda, as provisional head of state. An aristocrat and well-connected among the circles which brought about Villegas' downfall, Londoño is widely respected throughout the party as a unifying, unambitious figure. In his inauguration speech, he acknowledged the crisis in the party and vowed to steer the ship of state into calm waters, where someone else will be able to succeed him.
strings.COL_News.47.a: And how long will that be?
strings.COL_News.47.b: Hopefully they can settle their differences peacefully.
strings.COL_News.47.c: When spineless men lead, the whole community is cast adrift.
strings.COL_News.47.d: At least they're not killing each other again...“
strings.COL_News.48.desc:
Following failures to combat insurgencies in northern and eastern New Granada, President Augusto Ramírez Moreno has been removed via a military coup. General Hernando Forero Gómez took control of the nation, dissolving the national assembly, and making the military and national police the sole authority to fight against the insurgency.

Gómez's control is not absolute, as General Hernando Currea Cubides has declared himself an interim president. Currea has assured the government and public that he intends to return the nation to normalcy. It is unknown whether or not he will try and ride his momentum to become president, or surrender power back to the party.
strings.COL_News.48.a: That's our third... no... fourth man!
strings.COL_News.48.b: Can they just get it under control?
strings.COL_News.49.t: {get_newspaper_header}Hernán Jaramillo Ocampo Appointed as Moreno's Successor
strings.COL_News.49.desc:
Augusto Ramírez Moreno has resigned from his role as President of New Granada, following the death of his son. After a steady departure from politics, his new successor has been announced to be Hernán Jaramillo Ocampo, a skilled economist within the New Granadan government.

Ocampo has been dubbed an aloof figure by most, while also being praised for sustaining relationships with the coffee barons of his department of Caldas. His proposals on increasing Colombia's industrial development has raised eyebrows within the party.

Despite the suspicion, his economic approach has yielded stability and economic growth in the wartorn region. Time will only tell if this economist will be able to handle the reins of New Granada.
strings.COL_News.49.a: As long as I get my Folgers...
strings.COL_News.50.desc:
Augusto Ramírez Moreno has officially resigned as President of New Granada, citing the assassination of his son as the primary reason for his departure from office. His withdrawal from politics has been expected by many, although most didn't think it would take as long as it has.. Following a short ceremony, New Granada declared his new successor, Belisario Betancur Cuartas.

Betancur is seen as an inheritor of some of Laureano Gómez's ideals. One of 22 children from a poor family, Betancur has concerns for the embetterment of the common people of Colombia, and has stated that his primary focus as President will be directing the state to improve living conditions for the impoverished.
strings.COL_News.51.desc:
Following an unprecedented campaign of property nationalization and internal purges, President Silvio Villegas has announced his resignation, citing the “completion of the Revolutionary Traditionalist doctrine” envisioned by him and the other Leopardos in the 1920s.

Following Villegas' resignation, the reorganized ANP has elected his second-in-command, Hernán Jaramillo Ocampo as President. Party insiders have described Jaramillo as a stubborn and authoritarian man, a nationalist, yet one well-rooted in the Caldas oligarchy. Villegas' success will now allow him to have unprecedented control over the Colombian economy and political sphere. With this stable and firm hand, it is expected that Jaramillo will continue his predecessor's work and further mold the country in the image of its new masters.
strings.COL_News.51.a: Colombia falls further down the abyss.
strings.COL_News.51.b: Villegas has succeeded in tearing off Colombia's shackles.
strings.COL_News.51.c: The strong make their own future.
strings.COL_News.51.d: Who's ever heard of a fascist retiring of their own free will?
strings.COL_News.52.t: {get_newspaper_header}Castor Jaramillo Forms a New Government in Nueva Granada
strings.COL_News.52.desc:
When Colombian President Silvio Villegas announced his intent to nationalize all industries represented in the Supreme Economic Council, he had kicked off months of economic turmoil and political uproar. This crisis appears to have been concluded with a vote of no confidence by the Grand Council, leading to Villegas's ouster and a thorough purge of his allies in the administration.

Following these developments, Castor Jaramillo has now been sworn in as the new Colombian President. In his inauguration speech, he has proclaimed his intent to cooperate with the Colombian aristocracy, signalling a sea change in the Granadan ruling party's policy. The aristocracy of the old republic has managed to entrench not only its economic power over the new state, but also its political grip, rapidly erasing the lines between state and business.
strings.COL_News.52.c: Capital continues to chain the weak.
strings.COL_News.52.d: All this, just to return to the old republic?
strings.COL_News.53.t: {get_newspaper_header}The Interim Government Steps Down in Colombia
strings.COL_News.53.desc:
For the last few months, observers and governments have watched the spiraling protests and strikes in Colombia with growing concern, fearing them to be a portend for something worse. These fears have been disproven today as negotiations between the government and protesters have finally borne fruit, with Camader conceding his position and resigning. In his place, the National Assembly has appointed Guillermo León Valencia as his successor.

The face of Colombian conservatism, Valencia has long been an ally to the oligarchy, and his appointment signals that Camader's resignation may be as far as concessions go. Valencia's devout religiosity and his relative popularity has provided his ascendancy some much-needed legitimacy. Whether this can translate into stability and protecting the Partido Nacional's interests, however, are a different matter entirely.
strings.COL_News.53.a: The dove returns, carrying an olive leaf. But is the leaf truly new?
strings.COL_News.54.t: {get_newspaper_header}The Interim Government Steps Down in Colombia
strings.COL_News.54.desc:
For the last few months, observers and governments have watched the spiraling protests and strikes in Colombia with growing concern, fearing them to be a portend for something worse. Those fears were affirmed as negotiations between the protestors and the government collapsed, and as the army turned to violently suppressing the protests through massacres, assassinations and arrests. Condemning the violence, President Zambrano announced his resignation, but the damage has been done.

With Zambrano out of power and much of the civilian administration resigning in horror and disgrace, General Hernando Currea Cubides is widely expected to take control of governance, and is unlikely to let it go. With Colombia exhausted by decades of political violence, it seems that the National Party's time in office is truly over, and that Currea's wing of Francoists are set to dominate Colombian politics for years to come.
strings.COL_News.54.a: A King, to be coronated in blood.
strings.COL_News.55.t: {get_newspaper_header}The Constitution of the Second Republic of Colombia is Passed
strings.COL_News.55.desc:
After much debate, the newly named Second Republic of Colombia has finalized and ratified a new constitution for the state. The new constitution restores gubernatorial elections, while the presidential position remains a purely legislative process. This also comes with an expansion of the president's powers such as an unlimited veto and the ability to appoint ministers without needing confirmation from the legislature, while also streamlining impeachment procedures to prevent executive overreach.

This new constitution comes during a time of economic renewal for Colombia. Due to the immense power of corporations in the still-healing Colombia, the constitution has granted protections and privileges to these companies, ensuring them with a tight grip on politics.

The incumbent president, Diego Garcés Giraldo, has announced that he will remain in the executive branch, despite the new constitution.
strings.COL_News.56.desc:
After being thrusted into power by the stormy politics of Colombia, it appears that interim President Fernando Londoño y Londoño has managed to calm the tempest. In a televised message, Londoño announced his resignation, claiming that the party had survived the crisis and that his duty was now complete. He will now retire to his family, ceding his position to a replacement determined by the party.

Shortly afterwards, a press communique by the ANP stated that Belisario Betancur has been appointed President by majority vote. A dedicated civil servant renowned for his focus on transparency and reformism, this choice has signalled that the party may be relaxing its tight grasp on power. Belisario's compromising nature, as shown in his inaugural speech, is a far cry from the methods of his predecessors, one eagerly sought by a war-torn country.
strings.COL_News.56.a: A new era, or just a new facade?
strings.COL_News.56.b: A strong man, but can he deliver?
strings.COL_News.56.c: Maybe a strong hand could pull Colombia from its quagmire.
strings.COL_News.57.desc:
After being thrusted into power by the stormy politics of Colombia, it appears that interim President Fernando Londoño y Londoño has managed to calm the tempest. In a televised message, Londoño announced his resignation, claiming that the party had survived the crisis and that his duty was now complete. He will now retire to his family, ceding his position to a replacement determined by the party.

Almost immediately, the ANP has published a note commending Londoño for his exemplary service to the nation, and informing the country of the decision to appoint Hernán Jaramillo as President. Jaramillo is known as a stubborn and authoritarian man, and a close ally of the rural elites of his native Caldas. Jaramillo has promised to use technocratic expertise to achieve the renewed economic growth that eluded his predecessor, whilst continuing to institutionalize the ANP's reign in all aspects of national life.
strings.COL_News.57.a: The coils of fascism tighten around Colombia.
strings.COL_News.57.c: Maybe a strong hand could pull Colombia from its quagmire.
strings.COL_News.57.d: To new times, the same ones.
strings.COL_News.58.desc:
The house of cards has finally collapsed in Colombia. In the wake of mass protests over the government's refusal to efficiently deal with the ongoing insurgency, protests were quickly suppressed. However, in the wake of mass resignations, this has only guaranteed the collapse of the past government, with the military now wasting no time in implementing martial law, and rapidly entrenching their newfound position.

The coup, orchestrated by General Hernando Currea Cubides, has officially rejected some of the tendencies embraced by his predecessor, instead declaring a newfound support for Franco and promising a return to normalcy under the steady hand of the military, with Cubides himself officially declaring a provisional government. Few, however, know where this hand will end, and whether Colombia will see any genuine moves back to a civilian government.
strings.COL_News.58.a: A raven flies overhead, promising peace through its brambles.
strings.COL_News.59.desc:
The fires burn yet brighter. For years, Colombia has been wracked by instability and warfare, and that pattern has been extended yet further. Frustrated by moves interpreted as weakening the strength of the government and continued failures in quashing the socialist and nationalist insurgencies, Supreme Commander Hernando Forero Gómez has staged a coup, supported by the military and police detachments.

Whilst the ministries lurch through with little immediate guidance, few debate the intentions of Forero himself. Opening his first speech by condemning the perceived degeneracy of the outgoing regime, he pledged that he would guarantee the implementation of Falangism within a stable Colombia, and to end the long-running violence plaguing Colombia. Whether he can fulfil those promises or not, or if the military will ever stop marching down the streets of Bogotá, one thing is clear:
strings.COL_News.59.a: The Chief Torturer's eyes now hungrily search nationwide.
strings.COL_News.60.desc:
The tendrils dig deeper into Bogotá. Many may have been taken aback by the events surrounding Currea's initial coup, but few would be surprised by the results of his latest speech. Citing concerns over continued terrorism and accusations of continued subversion, General Hernando Currea Cubides announced in a televised speech that the High Military Council would indefinitely continue its governance.

Most remaining dissent to Currea's plans have been mute, but the implications are clear, with the ANP will be sidelined, with the military and Catholic Church to share power. Reception to these developments have been muted internationally, barring the Iberian Peninsula, which has offered its commendations to the new regime, and cardinals within the Catholic Church have provided quiet hopes that their new, central role will be important for the regime's development.
strings.COL_News.61.desc:
The leaves have been felled, leaving nothing but trunks. Few observers have been surprised as Supreme Commander Hernando Forero Gómez's efforts to install a military junta have come to fruition. Despite some measured resistance over the past months, it is now clear that the last embers of an internal power struggle between the ANP have been silenced by the guns and truncheons of the Colombian Military.

With an established reputation as a particularly brutal commander, his political sympathies have long been noted as being slavishly devoted to that of Falangism, a view he has only been too happy to foment. Now consolidating his power, it seems inevitable that he will seek to enforce ideological loyalty and purity across the Colombian Republic. If not through the barrel of the gun, then this will surely be enforced through the signing of a cheque.
strings.COL_News.61.a: The axe of the Fasces cut through the Amazon.
strings.COL_News.62.t: {get_newspaper_header}The Military Government Steps Down in Colombia
strings.COL_News.62.desc:
The sword may have been resheathed, but its glint still gleans. Announcing that the situation had been stabilized and that the need to oversee administrative order had faded, the military has officially announced the end of its junta, and a transition back to civilian rule. In response, the ANP has appointed Hernán Jaramillo Ocampo as President to succeed it.

The ANP's leading technocrat, Ocampo has already claimed a reputation as a secretive, authoritarian and stubborn figure, but will now be tested in the struggles against the pressures of an entrenched security apparatus, combined with widespread fatigue over factionalism. Whether Ocampo's reputation will truly precede him and will help him to secure his vision, or if the military will continue to intervene, has yet to be seen.
strings.COL_News.62.a: The vultures have selected their wolf.
strings.COL_News.63.t: {get_newspaper_header}The Military Government Steps Down in Colombia
strings.COL_News.63.desc:
The sword may have been resheathed, but its glint still gleans. Announcing that the situation had been stabilized and that the need to oversee administrative order had faded, the military has officially announced the end of its junta, and a transition back to civilian rule. In response, the ANP has appointed Belisario Betancur Cuartas as President to succeed it.

A scion of Moreno's reformist bloc, Belisario has been regarded as a relatively transparent and diplomatic man capable of maintaining the rough sense of stability felt within Colombia, and will likely loosen some of the tighter mechanisms of administrative repression. However, even with the handover, the military and security apparatus remain strong and continually overstep their bounds, a matter that will likely continue to exacerbate tensions throughout his administration.
strings.COL_News.64.desc:
A tense, weeks-long power struggle behind the scenes of the new government of the State of Colombia has burst into the open today with the arrest of José Camacho Carreño and the outlawing of the Nacional-Americanista movement. In a press statement, President Alfonso Uribe Misas claimed that the security services have unearthed a plot by Camacho and his associates to assassinate him, and denounced him as a traitor.

While the government has attempted to keep a tight lid on the affair, it is believed that the origin of the dispute lies in Misas' intentions to rehabilitate the Conservative party and slowly rebuild the structures of the old republic, leading the radical Nacional-Americanistas to break with his regime. Now, however - it seems the path forward is paved for Misas to take the crown of Bogotá's deposed leaders and mold it in his image.
strings.COL_News.64.a: As usual, the fascists can never settle their differences peacefully.
strings.COL_News.64.b: A long knife must be kept sharp.
strings.COL_News.65.desc:
While open warfare in Colombia has ended, it seems that political violence continues to determine its path. Today, the new Colombian government has been violently overthrown by militants connected to the radical Nacional-Americanista movement. The movement's leader, José Camacho Carreño, has announced the death of former president Alfonso Uribe Misas and the “beginning of a National Revolution”, proclaiming the Free State of Colombia.

Camacho, a former member of the Leopardos and of the Conservative party, has long been known as a radical, and his reputation for indulgent habits was only worsened by his time in prison for the murder of his brother-in-law and for political radicalism. Despite his unquestioned intellectual ability and economic knowledge, it is believed that German policy towards Colombia may shift due to Camacho's tendency towards erratic decision making, though there has been no comment yet from Europe.
strings.COL_News.65.a: Just when you thought it couldn't get worse...
strings.COL_News.65.b: What does he think he's doing?
strings.COL_News.65.c: Will Colombia drown in blood once more?
strings.COL_News.66.desc:
With the internal situation growing increasingly out of Bogotá's control and armed conflict once more ravaging Colombia, reports have now come in of the army dismissing President Camacho and his cabinet, with functions delegated to the State Council and the Nacional-Americanista movement purged. General Diógenes Gil has proclaimed an 'end to chaos and a return to normalcy', despite the gunfire still ringing in parts of the city.

The news comes after a meeting between Camacho and the German ambassador to Colombia over the supply of coffee and other crucial commodities to Germany has apparently ended in failure, leading many to believe that the Abwehr had a hand in the coup's organization. Eyewitnesses have even stated that alleged Colombian-German agent Heriberto Schwartau was present among the followers of General Gil during the execution of the putsch.
strings.COL_News.66.a: Try getting extreme nationalists to work together...

strings.COL_GranColombia.3.desc:
DIRECCIÓN FEDERAL DE SEGURIDAD
ISSUE: Growing Hostilities Between Venezuela and Colombia

Ever since the conclusion of the Colombian Civil War, tensions between Colombia and nearby Venezuela have been on a troubling incline. With an increase in the military presence along their border and public verbal bars between either nation's military leaders, foreign speculators worry of a possible armed incursion along the northern Andes.

For generations now, ideological divisions between Bogotá and Caracas have been more or less the norm. After Colombia's recent civil war, however, reconstruction has been slow to address social issues that have exacerbated the divide between the two nations, from post-war poverty prompting immigration to Venezuela to growing restlessness in the Colombian interior.

In addition, the Colombian Civil War provided ample cover for recent attempts to stage insurrection in Venezuela, with foreign-backed agitators hoping to use the violence to smuggle themselves over the border to facilitate regime change. This hasn't endeared Caracas to Colombia's post-war plight and has helped fuel further division.

Observers have noted that the possibility of war between Colombia and Venezuela, at least for now, is not likely. It is hoped that this status quo might continue for the duration. In the event of Colombiano/Venezuelano relations deteriorating further, a war in the northern Andes would prove to be just as, if not more bloody, than the Colombian Civil War. Recommend continued observation as the situation develops.

Very respectfully,
The Federal Director of Security
Captain Gutiérrez Barrios
strings.COL_GranColombia.4.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL

FROM AGENT TORINO
MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

SUBJECT: RISING TENSIONS BETWEEN COLOMBIA AND VENEZUELA

1. Ever since the dissolution of Gran Colombia in 1831, Venezuela's relationship with Colombia has been marred by controversy rooted in cultural divisions between Bogotá and Caracas. In recent years, with the conflicting interests of the Cold War converging in the recent Colombian Civil War, Venezuela's relationship with Colombia has taken a turn for the worse.

2. The post-war situation in Colombia has seen systemic poverty spike with poorer migrants emigrating over the Venezuelan border, becoming a long-term issue for the government in Caracas. The simmering tensions in Colombia, via lingering trauma from the Civil War, have seeded unease among the general population.

3. Over the past few months, growing animosity between the governments of Caracas and Bogotá has become increasingly front-facing, with heightened military activity along their mutual border. Military leaders on either side have openly begun positioning forces in opposition to the other, agitating their respective governments to reach a proper resolution.

4. Initial speculation suggests that war between Colombia and Venezuela is unlikely at the current time, but the situation is still malleable. Prospects for a protracted conflict in the North Andes are grim to say the least. With the recent attempts by foreign powers to use the Colombian Civil War for power plays in both Bogotá and Caracas, the best course of action would be to monitor the situation for the duration.
strings.COL_GranColombia.5.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL
To the Council of Ministers

Colombia - Post-Civil War Aftermath - Under Influence By Multiple Foreign PowersIt is well-known that the post-war reconstruction following the Colombian Civil War has been a patchwork affair, with entrenched poverty and murmurs of discontent stemming from both damage to the Colombian economy and long-term political reorganization. This has had the knock-on effect most pressingly with Colombia's northeastern neighbor, Venezuela.

Venezuela's exposure to the prelude, onset, and aftermath of the Colombian Civil War has fed into national and ideological differences between Venezuela and Colombia that have existed since Simón Bolívar's revolution. Adding to this, the economic situation in Colombia has led to an exodus of low-income Colombians to Venezuela, becoming a burden to their economy as well.

Foreign actors are known to have used the violence of the Civil War as cover to seed regime change in Venezuela (See attached folder). Combining this with the strain on Venezuela's economy has led to growing tension between Bogotá and Caracas, including public demands for action from their military leaders as well as a surge in military maneuvers along their borders.

Analysis of the tensions between Colombia and Venezuela seems to suggest that war is still a long way away. The violence of the Colombian Civil War is well-documented, and one can assume that neither Caracas nor Bogotá is in much of a hurry to invite another conflict thus far, but that can change should the situation not improve. Keeping tabs on these affairs would indeed be in our best interests.
strings.COL_GranColombia.6.desc:
TOP SECRET
EYES ONLY
TO ALL MEMBERS OF THE {getintelagencycaps}

COLOMBIA - POST-CIVIL WAR AFTERMATH - UNDER INFLUENCE BY MULTIPLE FOREIGN POWERS

The leadership of Venezuela has become increasingly antagonistic towards neighboring Colombia, with Bogotá's own enmity towards Caracas becoming incrementally mutual. The military presence on both sides has been steadily increasing, as have the demands for an immediate solution from their military leaders.

The Colombian Civil War left the economy in tatters, with reconstruction efforts slow to redress the damage. Poverty in the Colombian interior is high, coupled with trepidation from the population in the wake of the Civil War. This has led many to immigrate to Venezuela, leading to economic issues and resentment between the two.

Foreign interests from abroad have sought to exploit the Civil War in Colombia to attempt to spark similar events in Venezuela, using the violence from the fighting to back political dissidents and smuggle them over the border for their own ends (See attached file). This has only served to feed further animosity between the leadership of Caracas and Bogotá.

Open conflict between Colombia and Venezuela remains improbable. With recovery efforts in Colombia still ongoing and Venezuela still dealing with the fallout of recent political turmoil, potential warfare would only arise if the current relationship between Bogotá and Caracas deteriorates further. Ongoing surveillance of these events will proceed uninterrupted.

MAY GERMANY BE IN SAFE HANDS.
